Title: Behind the Myth of Exploration in Policy Gradients

Abstract:
Policy-gradient algorithms are reinforcement learning methods for control problems with continuous state and action spaces. In practice, exploration terms are included in the learning objective. The effectiveness of these terms is often justified by a need to explore environments. This analysis distinguishes two implications of these techniques. First, they can smooth the learning objective and eliminate local optima while preserving the global maximum. Second, they modify gradient estimates, increasing the probability that stochastic parameter updates provide an optimal policy. The effects of exploration strategies based on entropy bonuses are discussed and illustrated empirically, highlighting limitations and avenues for future work.

1 Introduction
Reinforcement learning solves sequential decision-making problems to minimize cost or maximize reward. It has been applied to tasks including playing games (Mnih et al., 2015; Silver et al., 2017), managing power systems (Aittahar et al., 2014), controlling robots (Kalashnikov et al., 2018), and interacting with electricity markets (Boukas et al., 2021).

Reinforcement learning algorithms include model-based, value-based, and policy-based methods. Model-based and value-based methods are subject to the exploration-exploitation dilemma during learning (Dann et al., 2017; Azar et al., 2017; Neu et al., 2020). For policy-based methods, specifically policy-gradient algorithms (Duan et al., 2016; Andrychowicz et al., 2020), a theoretical requirement for convergence toward optimal solutions is that policies remain sufficiently stochastic during learning (Bhandari & Russo, 2019; Bhatt et al., 2019; Agarwal et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Bedi et al., 2022). Stochastic policies have smoother returns (Ahmed et al., 2019; Bolland et al., 2023), but neither softmax nor Gaussian policies guarantee sufficient stochasticity for ensuring convergence (Mei et al., 2020; Mei et al., 2021; Bedi et al., 2022). This requirement is often called exploration.

Practitioners promote sufficient randomness in policies via reward-shaping strategies, optimizing a surrogate learning objective with reward bonuses. These bonuses promote actions that reduce uncertainty about the environment (Pathak et al., 2017; Burda et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021) or maximize the entropy of states and/or actions (Bellemare et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2021; Williams, 1991; Haarnoja et al., 2019). Optimizing a surrogate objective is effective for tasks with complex dynamics, complex reward functions, or sparse rewards (Islam et al., 2019; Lee et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2021).

Differences between theory and practice have led to folklore explaining policy-gradient methods. This work studies the maximization of practical surrogate learning objective functions from an optimization perspective. Studies of entropy regularization, an exploration-based reward shaping technique, include Ahmed et al. (2019), who concluded it helps provide smooth learning objective functions. The same strategy was reinterpreted as a robust optimization method by Husain et al. (2021) and as a two-player game by Brekelmans et al. (2022). Bolland et al. (2023) argued that optimizing an entropy regularized objective is equivalent to optimizing the return of another policy with larger variance. Chung et al. (2021) studied the effect of including baselines in policy gradient. These studies are specific to some exploration methods; unified explanations about exploration in policy-gradient methods are lacking.

The convergence of stochastic ascent methods is driven by the objective function and how ascent directions are estimated. The objective function should be (pseudo) concave to find its global maximum (Leon et al., 1998). The convergence rate is influenced by the distribution of stochastic ascent estimates (Chen et al., 2018; Ajalloeian & Stich, 2020). This paper studies policy-gradient methods with exploration-based reward shaping through these two optimization aspects. First, it discusses the effect of exploration on the learning objective and the relationship between an optimal policy and a policy maximizing the learning objective. Second, it elaborates on the distribution of gradient estimates of the learning objective and its likelihood of providing a direction in which the learning objective and return increase. Common exploration strategies are illustrated with respect to these aspects. A general framework for study and interpretation is introduced instead of finding the best exploration method for a given task.

The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 provides background. Section 3 studies the learning objective. Section 4 studies the ascent direction distribution. Section 5 concludes.

2 Background
This section introduces the reinforcement learning problem in Markov decision processes and discusses policy-gradient optimization with exploration.

2.1 Markov Decision Processes
Problems involve an agent making sequential decisions in a stochastic environment to maximize an expected sum of rewards (Sutton & Barto, 2018). The environment is modeled with an infinite-time Markov Decision Process (MDP) composed of a state space S, an action space A, an initial state distribution with density p0, a transition distribution with conditional density p, a bounded reward function ρ, and a discount factor γ ∈ [0,1). When an agent interacts, an initial state s0 ∼ p0(·) is sampled. At each time step t, the agent provides an action at ∈ A leading to a new state s_{t+1} ∼ p(·|s_t, a_t). A sequence of states and actions h_t = (s_0, a_0, …, s_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, s_t) ∈ H is a history; H is the set of all histories. After action a_t is executed, a reward r_t = ρ(s_t, a_t) ∈ R is observed.

A policy π ∈ Π = S → P(A) maps the state space S to the set of probability measures on the action space P(A), where π(a|s) is the conditional probability density of action a in state s. The function J:Π → R maps any policy π to the expected discounted sum of rewards gathered by an agent interacting in the MDP by sampling actions from π. The return of π is:
J(π) = (1/(1-γ)) E_{s∼d^{π,γ}(·), a∼π(·|s)}[ρ(s, a)],
where d^{π,γ}(·) is the discounted state-visitation probability (Manne, 1960). The goal is to find an optimal policy π* maximizing J.

2.2 Policy-Gradient Algorithms
Policy-gradient algorithms optimize a parameterized policy π_θ to find optimal parameter θ* maximizing J(π_{θ*}). Naively optimizing by maximizing return may provide sub-optimal results. Exploration strategies mitigate this by optimizing a surrogate learning objective L that encourages behaviors. Reward-shaping strategies extend the expected discounted sum of rewards by K additional intrinsic motivation terms ρ_i^{int}, optimizing:
L(θ) = (1/(1-γ)) E_{s∼d^{π_θ,γ}(·), a∼π_θ(·|s)}[ρ(s, a) + Σ_{i=0}^{K-1} λ_i ρ_i^{int}(s, a)] = J(π_θ) + J^{int}(π_θ),
where λ_i are non-negative weights and J^{int}(π_θ) is the intrinsic return. The parameter maximizing L is denoted θ†, distinguished from optimal policy parameter θ*. Intrinsic motivation terms are classified in two groups.

Uncertainty-based motivations: Provide bonuses for actions that reduce uncertainty about the environment (Pathak et al., 2017; Burda et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2021). Intrinsic motivation terms are proportional to prediction errors of a learned model of MDP dynamics.

Entropy-based motivations: Provide bonuses for visiting states and/or playing actions that are less likely in histories (Bellemare et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2019; Guo et al., 2021). This work focuses on two bonuses:
ρ^s(s, a) = - log d^{π_θ,γ}(φ(s))
ρ^a(s, a) = - log π_θ(a| s),
where φ(s) is a feature from state s. Corresponding intrinsic returns are maximized for policies that visit every feature uniformly, and for policies with uniformly distributed actions in each state, respectively. These rewards require estimating distributions over states and/or actions and depend on policy parameter θ. The second technique is entropy regularization (Williams, 1991; Haarnoja et al., 2019).

On-policy policy-gradient algorithms optimize differentiable parameterized policies with gradient-based local optimization (Duan et al., 2016; Andrychowicz et al., 2020). They iteratively approximate an ascent direction d̂ using histories sampled from the policy, updating parameters in the ascent direction or a combination of previous directions (Hinton et al., 2012; Kingma & Ba, 2014). For simplicity, ascent direction d̂ is composed of an estimate of the gradient of the return ĝ ≈ ∇_θ J(π_θ) and an estimate of the gradient of the intrinsic return î ≈ ∇_θ J^{int}(π_θ). The first is usually unbiased; the second is biased, typically neglecting the influence of the policy on the intrinsic reward.

3 Study of the Learning Objective
This section studies the influence of exploration terms on learning objective L. Two criteria are defined under which the learning objective can be globally optimized by ascent methods, and the solution is close to an optimal policy. Exploration modifies the learning objective to remove local extrema is graphically illustrated.

3.1 Policy-Gradient Learning Objective
Policy-gradient algorithms with exploration maximize L. Two criteria are introduced. First, a learning objective L is ε-coherent when its global maximum is in an ε-neighborhood of the return of an optimal policy. Second, learning objectives with a unique maximum and no other stationary point are pseudoconcave.

Coherence criterion: L is ε-coherent iff J(π_{θ*}) - J(π_{θ†}) ≤ ε, where θ* ∈ argmax_θ J(π_θ) and θ† ∈ argmax_θ L(θ).

Pseudoconcavity criterion: L is pseudoconcave iff ∃! θ†: ∇L(θ†) = 0 ∧ L(θ†) = max_θ L(θ).
If pseudoconcavity is respected, there is a single optimum, and the learning objective can be globally optimized by stochastic gradient ascent (Bottou et al., 2010). If L is ε-coherent, the solution is a near-optimal policy with suboptimality bound ε.

3.2 Illustration of the Effect of Exploration on the Learning Objective
Exploration is important with complex dynamics and reward functions where many locally optimal policies may exist (Lee et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). An environment and policy parameterization from Bolland et al. (2023) serve as an example. Learning objectives for different exploration strategies are represented, depicting global and local optima. Learning objectives with a single global optimum respect pseudoconcavity. The neighborhood Ω of optimal policy parameters is represented; any learning objective with its global maximum within Ω is coherent for a given ε. The policy parameter computed by stochastic gradient ascent is elaborated.

Consider the environment in Figure 1a where a car moves in a valley. State s=(x, v) with position x and speed v. The valley contains two separate low points at x_initial=-3 and x_target=3, separated by a peak. The car starts at rest v_0=0 at x_0=x_initial. Rewards are proportional to valley depth at current position; the reward function is in Figure 1b. Policy π_{K,σ}(a| s) = N(a| μ_K(s), σ) is a normally disturbed proportional controller with μ_K(s) = K×(x - x_target), parameterized by θ=(K, σ). Figure 1c illustrates the contour map of J(π_θ) as a function of K and σ. Optimal parameters (black dot) drive the car to pass the peak and reach the lowest valley floor at x_target. Green area represents set Ω = { θ' | max_θ J(π_θ) - J(π_{θ'}) ≤ ε } for ε=1.

Figure 2 illustrates learning objectives combining intrinsic rewards with different weights λ_1 and λ_2. Feature φ(s)=x. For weights approaching zero, parameter θ† maximizing L (black dot) corresponds to a policy with high return, in Ω, so ε-coherence is guaranteed for ε=1. Larger weights require larger ε for ε-coherence. Increasing weights, the learning objective eventually becomes pseudoconcave. There is a trade-off. In Figure 2b, a learning objective respects pseudoconcavity and ε-coherence for ε=1; a single global maximum (black dot) is in Ω.

Shaping reward with exploration based on state-visitation entropy appears good for optimizing policy. A drawback is reward depends on policy and its gradient computation requires estimating a complex probability measure. In this example, intrinsic reward was estimated by Monte-Carlo sampling for every parameter, which does not scale and requires approximations (Islam et al., 2019).

Observations suggest well-chosen exploration strategies can lead to learning objectives satisfying both criteria, guaranteeing policies suboptimal by at most ε can be computed by local optimization. When designing exploration strategies, the learning objective is modified for algorithms to converge to optimal policy parameters, achieved when both criteria are respected. Strategies like enforcing entropy can be effective but are heuristic. Both criteria may be subject to a trade-off. In complex environments, an efficient exploration strategy may require balancing criteria, e.g., through a schedule on weights.

4 Study of the Ascent Direction Distribution
Optimizing pseudoconcave functions with stochastic ascent methods converges under assumptions on gradient estimate distributions (Bottou et al., 2010; Chen et al., 2018; Ajalloeian & Stich, 2020). This section studies the influence of exploration terms on this distribution for policy gradients. The probability of improving the learning objective should be sufficiently large for efficiency. This is formalized and illustrated; exploration strategies can increase this probability.

4.1 Policy-Gradient Estimated Ascent Direction
Gradient ascent algorithms update parameters in direction d̂ to locally improve objective f. Quality can be studied (for small step size α→0) through random variable representing objective increase:
X = f(θ + α d̂) - f(θ) = α ⟨d̂, ∇_θ f(θ)⟩.
This variable depends on random event d̂ estimated by Monte-Carlo. Convergence can be studied by deriving upper bounds on E[X]. Instead, distributions P(‖X‖) and P(X > 0) are elaborated. P(X > 0) quantifies when ascent step improves objective. Assume P(X > 0) is sufficient to measure efficiency; all ascent steps lead to constant variation, so rate of policy improvement is proportional to P(X > 0).

For policy gradient, assume learning objectives respect previous criteria. Two new criteria are introduced. First, an exploration strategy is δ-efficient iff following ascent direction d̂ ≈ ∇_θ L(θ) has probability at least δ to increase L(θ) almost everywhere. Second, an exploration strategy is δ-attractive iff ∃ neighborhood of θ† containing parameter θ^{int} maximizing J^{int}, where probability of increasing return by following d̂ is almost everywhere at least δ. Each probability measure and random variable is a function of θ.

Efficiency criterion: An exploration strategy is δ-efficient iff ∀^∞ θ: P(D > 0) ≥ δ, where D = ⟨d̂, ∇_θ L(θ)⟩.

Attraction criterion: An exploration strategy is δ-attractive iff ∃ B(θ†): θ^{int} ∈ B(θ†), such that ∀^∞ θ ∈ B(θ†): P(G > 0) ≥ δ, where θ^{int} = argmax_θ J^{int}(π_θ), B(θ†) is a ball centered at θ†, and G = ⟨d̂, ∇_θ J(π_θ)⟩.

Efficiency criterion quantifies how often a stochastic gradient ascent step improves L. Attraction criterion rationale: in many exploration strategies, intrinsic reward is dense, so optimizing intrinsic return is presumably easy, meaning P(⟨î, ∇_θ J^{int}(π_θ)⟩ > 0). It implies easy local improvement of L by increasing intrinsic motivation terms. Policy-gradient algorithms may converge toward θ^{int} rather than θ† when P(⟨d̂, ∇_θ J(π_θ)⟩ > 0) is small. If criterion respected for large δ, this is less likely as policy gradients will tend to improve return if it approaches θ^{int} and enters B(θ†); eventually converging toward θ†.

4.2 Illustration of the Effect of Exploration on the Estimated Ascent Direction
Exploration is promoted for problems with sparse rewards, e.g., maze-environments (Islam et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2021; Guo et al., 2021). A maze-environment with sparse rewards is introduced to illustrate influence of exploration on gradient estimates. Two learning objective functions are presented; influence on performance is elaborated in light of efficiency and attraction criteria.

Consider a maze-environment: horizontal corridor of S=15 tiles. State s ∈ {1,…,S}. Actions: left a=-1 or right a=+1. When action taken, agent stays idle with probability p=0.7, moves with probability 0.3 in direction indicated, then s' = min(S, max(1, s + a)). Agent starts in s=1; target state s=S=15 is absorbing. Zero rewards except when reaching target state, reward r=100. Discount factor γ=0.99. Policy goes right with probability θ, left with probability 1-θ, density:
π_θ(a|s) = θ if a=1, 1-θ if a=-1.
Return J(π_θ) is in black in Figure 3a as function of θ, with two intrinsic returns: J^a(π_θ) (orange) and J^s(π_θ) (blue). Intrinsic rewards ρ^a(s, a) = - log π_θ(a| s) and ρ^s(s, a) = - log d^{π_θ,γ}(s) are used. Figure 3b illustrates J(π_θ) and two learning objectives: L^a(θ) and L^s(θ), using J^a(π_θ) and J^s(π_θ). J is pseudoconcave; optimal parameter θ*=1. Both learning objectives respect ε-coherence for ε=0, so θ* = θ†, and respect pseudoconcavity. There is no interest in optimizing L rather than J, as J is pseudoconcave. Choosing correct exploration strategy influences policy-gradient algorithms when building gradient estimates.

Estimates ĝ and d̂ are computed using REINFORCE (Williams, 1992) by sampling 8 histories of length T=100. In this environment, P(D > 0) equals P(G > 0), equal to probability derivative is positive. Figure 3c shows this probability for return and both learning objectives. Learning objectives are more efficient than return; they are δ-efficient for larger δ. Depending on parameter, L^a(θ) or L^s(θ) is best. For attraction criterion, intervals B^a = [θ^{int,a}, θ^{†,a}] and B^s = [θ^{int,s}, θ^{†,s}] are at top of Figure 3c. They are smallest balls containing maximizers of intrinsic return and learning objective. Let minima of orange and blue curves over intervals be δ^a and δ^s. Attraction criterion is respected for any δ ≤ δ^a and δ^s for L^a(θ) and L^s(θ). Computation of ĝ is zero when target not sampled, highly likely for policies with small θ. Adding exploration terms leads to policy-gradient algorithms that compute optimal policy more easily; naive optimization without exploration would fail or be sample inefficient.

Empirically, well-chosen exploration may remove local extrema and increase probability stochastic ascent steps improve objective. Under assumptions, this probability measures efficiency. Among learning objectives respecting coherence and pseudoconcavity, choose one with high δ in both efficiency and attraction criteria. REINFORCE estimates were used; considerations generalize to any reinforcement learning technique where exploration helps compute good estimates. Estimating a critic by stochastic gradient ascent suffers similarly.

This problem relates to overfitting or generalization. If same state-action pairs are repeatedly sampled with high probability, policy may appear optimal neglecting rewards in low-probability pairs. Gradient estimates will be zero with high probability; updates will not improve policy. In example, gradient estimates from policies with small θ wrongly indicate stationary point. 5 Conclusion
This research studies effects of exploration on performance of policy-gradient algorithms. Two effects are distinguished. First, exploration modifies learning objective to remove local extrema. Second, it modifies gradient estimates and increases likelihood update steps improve returns. These phenomena were studied through four criteria.

These ideas apply to other direct policy optimization algorithms. title: How Well Do Supervised 3D Models Transfer to Medical Imaging Tasks?
full_text:
\title{How Well Do Supervised 3D Models Transfer to Medical Imaging Tasks?}

\begin{abstract}
The pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm has become prominent in transfer learning. For example, if the model is pre-trained on ImageNet and then fine-tuned to PASCAL, it can significantly outperform that trained on PASCAL from scratch. While ImageNet pre-training has shown enormous success, it is formed in 2D, and the learned features are for classification tasks; when transferring to more diverse tasks, like 3D image segmentation, its performance is inevitably compromised due to the deviation from the original ImageNet context. A significant challenge lies in the lack of large, annotated 3D datasets rivaling the scale of ImageNet for model pre-training. To overcome this challenge, we make two contributions. Firstly, we construct AbdomenAtlas 1.1 that comprises **9,262** three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes with high-quality, per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven tumor types. Secondly, we develop a suite of models that are pre-trained on our AbdomenAtlas 1.1 for transfer learning. Our preliminary analyses indicate that the model trained only with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours has a transfer learning ability similar to the model trained with 5,050 (unlabeled) CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours. More importantly, the transfer learning ability of supervised models can further scale up with larger annotated datasets, achieving significantly better performance than preexisting pre-trained models, irrespective of their pre-training methodologies or data sources. We hope this study can facilitate collective efforts in constructing larger 3D medical datasets and more releases of supervised pre-trained models.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Pre-training and fine-tuning is a widely adopted transfer learning paradigm (Zoph et al., 2020). Given the relationship across different vision tasks, a model pre-trained on one dataset is expected to benefti another. Over the past few decades, pre-training has been important in AI development (Kumar, 2017; Radford et al., 2021). For 2D vision tasks, there are two available options: (i) supervised pre-training and $(i i)$ self-supervised pre-training, but for 3D vision tasks, option $(i)$ is often not available simply due to the lack of large, annotated 3D volumetric datasets (Wang et al., 2022).  

Supervised pre-training can learn image features that are transferable to many target tasks. It has been common practice to pre-train models using ImageNet and then fine-tune the model on target tasks that often have less training data, e.g., PASCAL. However, two challenges arise in ImageNet pre-training. Firstly, ImageNet predominantly comprises 2D images, leaving a palpable void in large-scale 3D datasets and investigation in 3D transfer learning (Huang et al., 2023). Secondly, ImageNet is intended for image classification, so the benefti for segmentation (and other vision tasks) can be somewhat compromised (He et al., 2019). If such an ImageNet-like dataset exists—formed in 3D and annotated per voxel—supervised pre-trained models are expected to transfer better to 3D image segmentation than self-supervised ones for two reasons.  

1. Supervised pre-training is more efficient in data and computation because of its explicit learning objective. While self-supervised pre-training can learn features without manual annotation, it often requires a large corpus of datasets (Xiao et al., 2022). Extracting meaningful features directly from raw, unlabeled data is inherently challenging. Unlabeled data have a high degree of redundancy (Haghighi et al., 2020; 2021) and noise (Mahajan et al., 2018), which can complicate the learning process. Therefore, self-supervised pre-training often calls for greater computational resources and time to match the outcomes achieved by supervised pre-training (Chen et al., 2020a; Tang et al., 2022). We have quantified the improved data and computational efficiency from perspectives of both pre-training (Figure 2a; $99.6\%$ fewer data) and fine-tuning (Figure 2b; $66\%$ less computation). Specifically, the model trained with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours shows transfer learning ability similar to that trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, highlighting the remarkable efficiency of supervised pre-training.  

2. Supervised pre-training enables the model to learn image features that are relevant to image segmentation. Self-supervised pre-training must extract images features from raw, unlabeled data using pretext tasks such as mask image modeling (Chen et al., 2019a; Tao et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2021b; He et al., 2022), instance discrimination (Xie et al., 2020; Chaitanya et al., 2020; Shekoofeh et al., 2021), etc. Despite their efficacy in pre-training, these pretext tasks share no obvious relation to the target image segmentation. In contrast, supervised pre-training uses semantically meaningful annotations (e.g., organ/tumor segmentation) as supervision, with which the model can mimic the behavior of medical professionals—identifying the edge and boundary of specific anatomical structures. As a result, the pre-training is interpretable, and the learned features are expected to be relevant to image segmentation tasks (Zamir et al., 2018; Ilharco et al., 2022; You et al., 2022). We have demonstrated that the learned features can be direct inference for organ segmentation on CT volumes collected from hospitals worldwide (Table 3; evaluated on three novel hospitals). The features learned by supervision can also be fine-tuned to perform novel class segmentation (unseen in the pre-training) with higher accuracy and less annotated data than the features learned by self-supervision (Table 4; evaluated on 63 novel classes).  

This paper seeks to answer the question how well the model transfers to 3D medical imaging tasks IF it is pre-trained on large, annotated 3D datasets. Naturally, we start with creating an $I F$ dataset at a massive scale. Firstly, we construct a dataset (termed AbdomenAtlas $1.1^{1}$ ) of 9,262 CT volumes with per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven types of tumors. This large-scale, fully-annotated dataset enables us to train models in a fully supervised manner using multi-organ segmentation as the pretext task. As reviewed in Table 1, this dataset is much more extensive (considering both the number of CT volumes and annotated classes) than public datasets (Wasserthal et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022; Qu et al., 2023). Scaling experiments in $\S3.1$ suggested that pre-training models on more annotated datasets can further improve the transfer learning ability. Secondly, we develop a suite of Supervised Pre-trained Models, termed SuPreM, that combined the good of large-scale datasets and per-voxel annotations, demonstrating the efficacy across a range of target segmentation tasks. As reported in $\S3.2$ , some of the dominant segmentation backbones have been pre-trained and will be available to the public. Current pre-trained backbones are U-Net (CNN-type) (Ronneberger et al., 2015), SegResNet (CNN-type) (Myronenko, 2019), and Swin UNETR (Transformer-type) (Tang et al., 2022), and more backbones will be added along time.  

In prospective endeavors, we anticipate that the expansion of datasets and annotations will not only enhance feature learning, as demonstrated in this study, but also promote the development of advanced AI algorithms and benchmark the state of the art in terms of segmentation performance, inference efficiency, and domain generalizability.  



\section{2 BRIEF HISTORY: SUPERVISED PRE-TRAINING  }


In a major initiative aimed at developing widely transferable AI models—known as Foundation Models in the medical domain (Moor et al., 2023; Butoi et al., 2023; Ma & Wang, 2023a)—one faces a critical decision: should the focus of pre-training be supervised or self-supervised? While human annotations undeniably improve task-specific performance, such as semantic segmentation, the best strategy for learning generic image features that can be transferable across a spectrum of tasks has yet to be determined. For 2D vision tasks, the advent of ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) makes it possible to debate the merits and limitations of supervised pre-trained models for transfer learning compared with self-supervised ones. We refer the readers to Yang et al. (2020) and Tendle & Hasan (2021) for a plethora of viewpoints from either side. In essence, the debates are about clarifying the learning objective (loss function) of emulating human vision (Zhou, 2021).  

The learning objective of supervised pre-training is to minimize the discrepancy between AI predictions and semantic labels annotated by humans. Over the years, supervised pre-training on ImageNet has shown marked success in transfer learning (Yosinski et al., 2014). Moreover, the transfer learning ability can be further enhanced when models are trained on increasingly expansive datasets, such as ImageNet-21K (Kolesnikov et al., 2020), Instagram (Mahajan et al., 2018), JFT-300M (Sun et al., 2017), and JFT-3B (Zhai et al., 2022). In general, supervised pre-training exhibits clear advantages over self-supervised pre-training when sizable annotated datasets are available (Steiner et al., 2021; Ridnik et al., 2021). However, acquiring millions of manual annotations is labor-intensive, timeconsuming, and challenging to scale—but certainly not impossible—evidenced by several recent influential endeavors (Kuznetsova et al., 2020; Mei et al., 2022; Kirillov et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023).  

On the other hand, self-supervised pre-training offers an alternative by enabling AI models to learn from raw, unlabeled data (Jing & Tian, 2020; Zoph et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022; 2023), thus reducing the need for manual annotation. Self-supervised pre-training has historically lagged behind the state-of-the-art supervised pre-training in ImageNet benchmarks (Pathak et al., 2016; Noroozi & Favaro, 2016). The recent pace of progress in self-supervised pre-training has yielded models whose performance not only matches but, at times, surpasses those achieved by supervised pre-training (Chen et al., 2020a; Grill et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020b; Zhou et al., 2021a; Wei et al., 2022). This has raised hopes that self-supervised pre-training could indeed replace the ubiquitous supervised pre-training in advanced computer vision going forward. The caveat, however, is the significant demand for both data and computational power, often exceeding the resources available in academic settings. For example, He et al. (2020) have demonstrated that self-supervised features trained on 1B images (a factor of $714\times$ larger) can transfer comparably or better than ImageNet features.  

Supervised pre-training on ImageNet has demonstrated benefit for 2D medical image tasks after transfer learning (Tajbakhsh et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2017). Unfortunately, it has been constrained for 3D medical imaging tasks due to the lack of a 3D counterpart to ImageNet. Although there are a great number of raw, unlabeled medical images available (Team, 2011; Baxter et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Saenz et al., 2024), annotating these images is a labor-intensive undertaking for professionals. Our contribution to a large, annotated 3D dataset could spark the debate of whether self-supervised or supervised pre-training leads to better performance and data/computational efficiency, which would not be possible without the invention of a dataset of such a scale.  



\section{3 MATERIAL & METHOD  }


We constructed an AbdomenAtlas 1.1 dataset comprising 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes and over 251,323 masks spanning 25 anatomical structures and 7 types of tumors. In addition, we released a suite of supervised pre-trained models (SuPreM) to benefit 3D medical imaging tasks.  



\section{3.1 EXTENSIVE DATASET: ABDOMENATLAS 1.1  }


Interactive segmentation, an integration of AI algorithms and human expertise, was used to create AbdomenAtlas 1.1 in a semi-automatic procedure. We recruited a team of ten radiologists to perform manual annotations to ensure the annotation quality2. Given the complexity of 3D data, rather than annotating the entire dataset voxel by voxel, we asked the radiologists to focus on the most important CT volumes and regions therein. In doing so, an importance score for each volume was computed, derived from the uncertainty, consistency, and overlap (Qu et al., 2023). Six junior radiologists revised the annotations predicted by AI under the supervision of four senior radiologists, and in turn, AI improved its predictions by learning from these revised annotations. This interactive procedure continued to enhance the quality of annotations until no major revision was required from the radiologists. Subsequently, four senior radiologists went through the final visualizations for all the annotations, detecting and revising major errors as needed before the dataset was released. Annotation tools employed included a licensed version from Pair and an open-source MONAI Label.

At the time this paper is written, neither supervised nor self-supervised pre-training has been performed on this scale of dataset (9,262 volumetric data)3. We have developed models (termed SuPreM) pre-trained on data and annotations in AbdomenAtlas 1.1, which leverage established CNN backbones, such as U-Net and SegResNet, as well as Transformer backbones, such as Swin UNETR. With the growing trend of using pre-trained models, we have maintained a standardized, accessible model repository for sharing public model weights as well as a suite of supervised pretrained models (SuPreM) released by us. \section{4.1 DATA, ANNOTATION, AND COMPUTATIONAL EFFICIENCY  }

Supervised pre-training beneftis from explicit annotations, which provide direct guidance for the task, i.e., segmentation in this study. The model learns features from both data and annotations, which offer strong and precise supervision. On the other hand, self-supervised learning relies on pretext tasks derived from the raw data, which may offer a more ambiguous learning signal, therefore requiring more examples to capture meaningful features. Importantly, our finding suggests that supervised pretraining is more scalable with increased data. When data are increased from 21 to 1,575 volumes, the transfer learning performance on TotalSegmentator improves from $90.4\%$ to $91.3\%$ . In comparison, for self-supervised pre-training, an increase in data from 1,000 to 5,050 volumes only marginally improves performance from $89.7\%$ to $89.9\%$ . Fine-tuning on novel classes. The value of transfer learning lies in fine-tuning the pre-trained models on novel scenarios (Zhou et al., 2021b), such as novel classes, image modalities, and vision tasks that are completely unseen during the pre-training. In this study, we evaluate the proficiency of SuPreM when transferred to a wide variety of novel classes for 3D image segmentation tasks4. These novel classes include 19 muscles, 15 cardiac structures, 5 organs, and 24 vertebrae from the TotalSegmentator dataset, as well as three fine-grained pancreatic tumor types from the proprietary dataset. As shown in Table 4, our SuPreM, supervised pre-trained on 25 classes, can transfer better to novel classes than those self-supervised models pre-trained on raw, unlabeled data. We find that the pretext task of segmentation itself can enhance the model capability of segmenting novel classes. The benefit of same-task transfer learning, i.e., segmentation as pretext and target tasks, is much more straightforward and understandable than other pretext tasks such as contextual prediction, mask image modeling, and instance discrimination. Through full supervision in segmentation tasks, the model learns to understand the concept of objectness5, wherein the model gains a more profound understanding of what characterizes an object. The model does not just recognize predefined objects but begins to understand the foundational factors of objects in general. Such factors include texture, boundary, shape, size, and other low-level visual cues that are often deemed essential for image segmentation. This resonates with our assertion in the introduction: just as classification-based features from ImageNet transfer optimally for classification tasks (Huh et al., 2016; He et al., 2019; Zoph et al., 2020; Ridnik et al., 2021), segmentation-based features are optimal for segmentation tasks. Our findings do not negate the value of self-supervised pre-training. With 9,262 CT volumes, should self-supervised pre-training outperforms supervised pre-training in model transferability in the future, its value will be further highlighted by eliminating the need for manual annotations.

This is particularly critical for tumor imaging tasks because annotating tumors requires much more effort and often relies on the availability of pathology reports.  



\section{5 CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION  }


This study examines the transfer learning ability of supervised models that are pre-trained on 3D annotated datasets and fine-tuned on 3D image segmentation tasks. We start by constructing AbdomenAtlas 1.1, an extensive collection of 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes with highquality, per-voxel annotations. The magnitude of this dataset is unprecedented regarding data volume (2,789,975 images), granularity of annotations (251,323 masks), and inclusive diversity (88 hospitals). This dataset facilitates the development of a suite of pre-trained models, termed SuPreM, that can be effectively transferred to a broad spectrum of 3D image segmentation tasks. Notably, SuPreM transfers better than all existing 3D models by a large margin, especially when transferred to under-annotated datasets. The model trained with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours shows a transfer learning ability similar to that trained with $5{,}050\,\mathrm{CT}$ volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, highlighting the remarkable efficiency of supervised pre-training. We also demonstrate that the learned features can direct inference effectively on external datasets and fine-tune to segment novel classes and classify multiple types of tumors with higher accuracy and less annotated data than those learned by self-supervision.

\title{How Well Do Supervised 3D Models Transfer to Medical Imaging Tasks?}

\begin{abstract}
The pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm has become prominent in transfer learning. For example, if the model is pre-trained on ImageNet and then fine-tuned to PASCAL, it can significantly outperform that trained on PASCAL from scratch. While ImageNet pre-training has shown enormous success, it is formed in 2D, and the learned features are for classification tasks; when transferring to more diverse tasks, like 3D image segmentation, its performance is inevitably compromised due to the deviation from the original ImageNet context. A significant challenge lies in the lack of large, annotated 3D datasets rivaling the scale of ImageNet for model pre-training. To overcome this challenge, we make two contributions. Firstly, we construct AbdomenAtlas 1.1 that comprises **9,262** three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes with high-quality, per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven tumor types. Secondly, we develop a suite of models that are pre-trained on our AbdomenAtlas 1.1 for transfer learning. Our preliminary analyses indicate that the model trained only with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours has a transfer learning ability similar to the model trained with 5,050 (unlabeled) CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours. More importantly, the transfer learning ability of supervised models can further scale up with larger annotated datasets, achieving significantly better performance than preexisting pre-trained models, irrespective of their pre-training methodologies or data sources. We hope this study can facilitate collective efforts in constructing larger 3D medical datasets and more releases of supervised pre-trained models.
\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }


Pre-training and fine-tuning is a widely adopted transfer learning paradigm (Zoph et al., 2020). Given the relationship across different vision tasks, a model pre-trained on one dataset is expected to benefti another. Over the past few decades, pre-training has been important in AI development (Kumar, 2017; Radford et al., 2021). For 2D vision tasks, there are two available options: (i) supervised pre-training and $(i i)$ self-supervised pre-training, but for 3D vision tasks, option $(i)$ is often not available simply due to the lack of large, annotated 3D volumetric datasets (Wang et al., 2022).  

Supervised pre-training can learn image features that are transferable to many target tasks. It has been common practice to pre-train models using ImageNet and then fine-tune the model on target tasks that often have less training data, e.g., PASCAL. However, two challenges arise in ImageNet pre-training. Firstly, ImageNet predominantly comprises 2D images, leaving a palpable void in large-scale 3D datasets and investigation in 3D transfer learning (Huang et al., 2023). Secondly, ImageNet is intended for image classification, so the benefti for segmentation (and other vision tasks) can be somewhat compromised (He et al., 2019). If such an ImageNet-like dataset exists—formed in 3D and annotated per voxel—supervised pre-trained models are expected to transfer better to 3D image segmentation than self-supervised ones for two reasons.  

1. Supervised pre-training is more efficient in data and computation because of its explicit learning objective. While self-supervised pre-training can learn features without manual annotation, it often requires a large corpus of datasets (Xiao et al., 2022). Extracting meaningful features directly from raw, unlabeled data is inherently challenging. Unlabeled data have a high degree of redundancy (Haghighi et al., 2020; 2021) and noise (Mahajan et al., 2018), which can complicate the learning process. Therefore, self-supervised pre-training often calls for greater computational resources and time to match the outcomes achieved by supervised pre-training (Chen et al., 2020a; Tang et al., 2022). We have quantified the improved data and computational efficiency from perspectives of both pre-training (Figure 2a; $99.6\%$ fewer data) and fine-tuning (Figure 2b; $66\%$ less computation). Specifically, the model trained with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours shows transfer learning ability similar to that trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, highlighting the remarkable efficiency of supervised pre-training.  

2. Supervised pre-training enables the model to learn image features that are relevant to image segmentation. Self-supervised pre-training must extract images features from raw, unlabeled data using pretext tasks such as mask image modeling (Chen et al., 2019a; Tao et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2021b; He et al., 2022), instance discrimination (Xie et al., 2020; Chaitanya et al., 2020; Shekoofeh et al., 2021), etc. Despite their efficacy in pre-training, these pretext tasks share no obvious relation to the target image segmentation. In contrast, supervised pre-training uses semantically meaningful annotations (e.g., organ/tumor segmentation) as supervision, with which the model can mimic the behavior of medical professionals—identifying the edge and boundary of specific anatomical structures. As a result, the pre-training is interpretable, and the learned features are expected to be relevant to image segmentation tasks (Zamir et al., 2018; Ilharco et al., 2022; You et al., 2022). We have demonstrated that the learned features can be direct inference for organ segmentation on CT volumes collected from hospitals worldwide (Table 3; evaluated on three novel hospitals). The features learned by supervision can also be fine-tuned to perform novel class segmentation (unseen in the pre-training) with higher accuracy and less annotated data than the features learned by self-supervision (Table 4; evaluated on 63 novel classes).  

This paper seeks to answer the question how well the model transfers to 3D medical imaging tasks IF it is pre-trained on large, annotated 3D datasets. Naturally, we start with creating an $I F$ dataset at a massive scale. Firstly, we construct a dataset (termed AbdomenAtlas $1.1^{1}$ ) of 9,262 CT volumes with per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven types of tumors. This large-scale, fully-annotated dataset enables us to train models in a fully supervised manner using multi-organ segmentation as the pretext task. As reviewed in Table 1, this dataset is much more extensive (considering both the number of CT volumes and annotated classes) than public datasets (Wasserthal et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022; Qu et al., 2023). Scaling experiments in $\S3.1$ suggested that pre-training models on more annotated datasets can further improve the transfer learning ability. Secondly, we develop a suite of Supervised Pre-trained Models, termed SuPreM, that combined the good of large-scale datasets and per-voxel annotations, demonstrating the efficacy across a range of target segmentation tasks. As reported in $\S3.2$ , some of the dominant segmentation backbones have been pre-trained and will be available to the public. Current pre-trained backbones are U-Net (CNN-type) (Ronneberger et al., 2015), SegResNet (CNN-type) (Myronenko, 2019), and Swin UNETR (Transformer-type) (Tang et al., 2022), and more backbones will be added along time.  

In prospective endeavors, we anticipate that the expansion of datasets and annotations will not only enhance feature learning, as demonstrated in this study, but also promote the development of advanced AI algorithms and benchmark the state of the art in terms of segmentation performance, inference efficiency, and domain generalizability.  



\section{2 BRIEF HISTORY: SUPERVISED PRE-TRAINING  }


In a major initiative aimed at developing widely transferable AI models—known as Foundation Models in the medical domain (Moor et al., 2023; Butoi et al., 2023; Ma & Wang, 2023a)—one faces a critical decision: should the focus of pre-training be supervised or self-supervised? While human annotations undeniably improve task-specific performance, such as semantic segmentation, the best strategy for learning generic image features that can be transferable across a spectrum of tasks has yet to be determined. For 2D vision tasks, the advent of ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) makes it possible to debate the merits and limitations of supervised pre-trained models for transfer learning compared with self-supervised ones. We refer the readers to Yang et al. (2020) and Tendle & Hasan (2021) for a plethora of viewpoints from either side. In essence, the debates are about clarifying the learning objective (loss function) of emulating human vision (Zhou, 2021).  

The learning objective of supervised pre-training is to minimize the discrepancy between AI predictions and semantic labels annotated by humans. Over the years, supervised pre-training on ImageNet has shown marked success in transfer learning (Yosinski et al., 2014). Moreover, the transfer learning ability can be further enhanced when models are trained on increasingly expansive datasets, such as ImageNet-21K (Kolesnikov et al., 2020), Instagram (Mahajan et al., 2018), JFT-300M (Sun et al., 2017), and JFT-3B (Zhai et al., 2022). In general, supervised pre-training exhibits clear advantages over self-supervised pre-training when sizable annotated datasets are available (Steiner et al., 2021; Ridnik et al., 2021). However, acquiring millions of manual annotations is labor-intensive, timeconsuming, and challenging to scale—but certainly not impossible—evidenced by several recent influential endeavors (Kuznetsova et al., 2020; Mei et al., 2022; Kirillov et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2023).  

On the other hand, self-supervised pre-training offers an alternative by enabling AI models to learn from raw, unlabeled data (Jing & Tian, 2020; Zoph et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022; 2023), thus reducing the need for manual annotation. Self-supervised pre-training has historically lagged behind the state-of-the-art supervised pre-training in ImageNet benchmarks (Pathak et al., 2016; Noroozi & Favaro, 2016). The recent pace of progress in self-supervised pre-training has yielded models whose performance not only matches but, at times, surpasses those achieved by supervised pre-training (Chen et al., 2020a; Grill et al., 2020; Chen et al., 2020b; Zhou et al., 2021a; Wei et al., 2022). This has raised hopes that self-supervised pre-training could indeed replace the ubiquitous supervised pre-training in advanced computer vision going forward. The caveat, however, is the significant demand for both data and computational power, often exceeding the resources available in academic settings. For example, He et al. (2020) have demonstrated that self-supervised features trained on 1B images (a factor of $714\times$ larger) can transfer comparably or better than ImageNet features.  

Supervised pre-training on ImageNet has demonstrated benefit for 2D medical image tasks after transfer learning (Tajbakhsh et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2016; Zhou et al., 2017). Unfortunately, it has been constrained for 3D medical imaging tasks due to the lack of a 3D counterpart to ImageNet. Although there are a great number of raw, unlabeled medical images available (Team, 2011; Baxter et al., 2023; Zhao et al., 2023; Saenz et al., 2024), annotating these images is a labor-intensive undertaking for professionals. Our contribution to a large, annotated 3D dataset could spark the debate of whether self-supervised or supervised pre-training leads to better performance and data/computational efficiency, which would not be possible without the invention of a dataset of such a scale.  



\section{3 MATERIAL & METHOD  }


We constructed an AbdomenAtlas 1.1 dataset comprising 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes and over 251,323 masks spanning 25 anatomical structures and 7 types of tumors. In addition, we released a suite of supervised pre-trained models (SuPreM) to benefit 3D medical imaging tasks.  



\section{3.1 EXTENSIVE DATASET: ABDOMENATLAS 1.1  }


Interactive segmentation, an integration of AI algorithms and human expertise, was used to create AbdomenAtlas 1.1 in a semi-automatic procedure. We recruited a team of ten radiologists to perform manual annotations to ensure the annotation quality2. Given the complexity of 3D data, rather than annotating the entire dataset voxel by voxel, we asked the radiologists to focus on the most important CT volumes and regions therein. In doing so, an importance score for each volume was computed, derived from the uncertainty, consistency, and overlap (Qu et al., 2023). Six junior radiologists revised the annotations predicted by AI under the supervision of four senior radiologists, and in turn, AI improved its predictions by learning from these revised annotations. This interactive procedure continued to enhance the quality of annotations until no major revision was required from the radiologists. Subsequently, four senior radiologists went through the final visualizations for all the annotations, detecting and revising major errors as needed before the dataset was released. Annotation tools employed included a licensed version from Pair and an open-source MONAI Label.

\section{4.1 DATA, ANNOTATION, AND COMPUTATIONAL EFFICIENCY  }


Summary. We demonstrate the remarkable efficiency: (1) SuPreM trained with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours shows transfer learning ability similar to that trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours. (2) SuPreM requires $50\%$ fewer manual annotations for organ/tumor segmentation than self-supervised pre-training.  

Data efficiency for pre-training. As shown in Figure 2a, supervised pre-training requires less data (21 vs. 5,050 CT volumes) for the pretext task than self-supervised pre-training. This discrepancy arises from the inherent differences in their learning learning objectives and the information they leverage. Supervised pre-training beneftis from explicit annotations, which provide direct guidance for the task, i.e., segmentation in this study. The model learns features from both data and annotations, which offer strong and precise supervision. On the other hand, self-supervised learning relies on pretext tasks derived from the raw data, which may offer a more ambiguous learning signal, therefore requiring more examples to capture meaningful features. Importantly, our finding suggests that supervised pretraining is more scalable with increased data. When data are increased from 21 to 1,575 volumes, the transfer learning performance on TotalSegmentator improves from $90.4\%$ to $91.3\%$ . In comparison, for self-supervised pre-training, an increase in data from 1,000 to 5,050 volumes only marginally improves performance from $89.7\%$ to $89.9\%$ . \section{4.2 ENHANCED FEATURES FOR NOVEL DATASETS, CLASSES, AND TASKS  }


Summary. The learned features manifest considerable generalizability and adaptability. The features can direct inference for organ segmentation on external datasets of CT volumes taken from different hospitals. The features can also be fine-tuned to segment novel organ/tumor classes and classify tumor sub-types with higher accuracy and less annotated data than those learned by self-supervision.  

Direct inference on external datasets. AI models trained on a specific dataset often encounter challenges in generalizing to novel datasets when a marked difference—referred to as a domain gap—exists between them (Zhang & Metaxas, 2023). While domain adaptation and generalization are prevalent research strategies to mitigate this challenge (Guan & Liu, 2021; Zhou et al.1). We assume the domain gap between CT volumes from different hospitals is not as pronounced as those in computer vision. This is because of the relatively standardized nature of computer tomography as an imaging modality, where pixel intensity conveys consistent anatomical significance (Zhou et al., 2022b). AbdomenAtlas 1.1 presents impressive diversity, covering CT volumes with variations in contrast enhancement, reconstruction kernels, CT scanner types, and acquisition parameters. This benefit is much more straightforward and understandable than such self-supervised tasks as contextual prediction, mask image modeling, and instance discrimination in the context of transfer learning. We hypothesize that it is because the model learns to understand the concept of objectness in a broader sense through full supervision, as suggested by Kirillov et al. For comparison, we also collect the result achieved by dataset-specific AI models—those individually trained on the specific datasets—referred to as independently and identically distributed (IID) performance. As shown in Table 3, our SuPreM can be generalized well to novel data distribution without the need for further fine-tuning or adaptation, consistently offering OOD performance that matches or even exceeds that of its IID counterparts.  

Fine-tuning on novel classes. The value of transfer learning lies in fine-tuning the pre-trained models on novel scenarios (Zhou et al., 2021b), such as novel classes, image modalities, and vision tasks that are completely unseen during the pre-training. In this study, we evaluate the proficiency of SuPreM when transferred to a wide variety of novel classes for 3D image segmentation tasks4. These novel classes include 19 muscles, 15 cardiac structures, 5 organs, and 24 vertebrae from the TotalSegmentator dataset, as well as three fine-grained pancreatic tumor types from the proprietary dataset. As shown in Table 4, our SuPreM, supervised pre-trained on 25 classes, can transfer better to novel classes than those self-supervised models pre-trained on raw, unlabeled data. We find that the pretext task of segmentation itself can enhance the model capability of segmenting novel classes. The benefit of same-task transfer learning, i.e., segmentation as pretext and target tasks, is much more straightforward and understandable than other pretext tasks such as contextual prediction, mask image modeling, and instance discrimination. Through full supervision in segmentation tasks, the model learns to understand the concept of objectness5, wherein the model gains a more profound understanding of what characterizes an object. The model does not just recognize predefined objects but begins to understand the foundational factors of objects in general. Such factors include texture, boundary, shape, size, and other low-level visual cues that are often deemed essential for image segmentation. This resonates with our assertion in the introduction: just as classification-based features from ImageNet transfer optimally for classification tasks (Huh et al., 2016; He et al., 2019; Zoph et al., 2020; Ridnik et al., 2021), segmentation-based features are optimal for segmentation tasks. Our findings do not negate the value of self-supervised pre-training. With 9,262 CT volumes, should self-supervised pre-training outperforms supervised pre-training in model transferability in the future, its value will be further highlighted by eliminating the need for manual annotations.

The distance between the two tasks is much larger than transferring among segmentation tasks. This is particularly critical for tumor imaging tasks because annotating tumors requires much more effort and often relies on the availability of pathology reports.  



\section{5 CONCLUSION AND DISCUSSION  }


This study examines the transfer learning ability of supervised models that are pre-trained on 3D annotated datasets and fine-tuned on 3D image segmentation tasks. We start by constructing AbdomenAtlas 1.1, an extensive collection of 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes with highquality, per-voxel annotations. The magnitude of this dataset is unprecedented regarding data volume (2,789,975 images), granularity of annotations (251,323 masks), and inclusive diversity (88 hospitals). This dataset facilitates the development of a suite of pre-trained models, termed SuPreM, that can be effectively transferred to a broad spectrum of 3D image segmentation tasks. Notably, SuPreM transfers better than all existing 3D models by a large margin, especially when transferred to under-annotated datasets. The model trained with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours shows a transfer learning ability similar to that trained with $5{,}050\,\mathrm{CT}$ volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, highlighting the remarkable efficiency of supervised pre-training. We also demonstrate that the learned features can direct inference effectively on external datasets and fine-tune to segment novel classes and classify multiple types of tumors with higher accuracy and less annotated data than those learned by self-supervision.

Title: How Well Do Supervised 3D Models Transfer to Medical Imaging Tasks?

Abstract:
The pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm is the dominant standard in transfer learning. For instance, a model pre-trained on ImageNet and then fine-tuned on PASCAL will always significantly outperform a model trained on PASCAL from scratch. While ImageNet pre-training has demonstrated enormous success, it is inherently limited to 2D imagery and classification tasks; its performance is fundamentally compromised when transferring to more diverse tasks like 3D image segmentation due to the significant deviation from the original ImageNet context. The primary obstacle has been the complete absence of large, annotated 3D datasets rivaling the scale of ImageNet for effective model pre-training. To overcome this critical challenge, we deliver two major contributions with immediate practical value. Firstly, we construct AbdomenAtlas 1.1, a definitive dataset comprising 9,262 three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes with high-quality, per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven tumor types. Secondly, we develop a comprehensive suite of models pre-trained on our AbdomenAtlas 1.1 for transfer learning. Our conclusive analyses prove that a model trained with only 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours achieves a transfer learning ability equivalent to a model trained with 5,050 (unlabeled) CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours. More importantly, the transfer learning ability of supervised models definitively scales up with larger annotated datasets, achieving vastly superior performance compared to all preexisting pre-trained models, regardless of their pre-training methodologies or data sources. This work establishes a new foundation for constructing larger 3D medical datasets and will directly accelerate the development and deployment of supervised pre-trained models in clinical practice.

1 INTRODUCTION

Pre-training and fine-tuning is the universally adopted transfer learning paradigm. Given the fundamental relationships across different vision tasks, a model pre-trained on one dataset is guaranteed to benefit another. Over the past decades, pre-training has been the cornerstone of AI development. For 2D vision tasks, two options exist: (i) supervised pre-training and (ii) self-supervised pre-training. However, for 3D vision tasks, option (i) has been entirely unavailable due to the complete lack of large, annotated 3D volumetric datasets.

Supervised pre-training directly learns image features that are inherently transferable to many target tasks. The standard practice is to pre-train models using ImageNet and then fine-tune on target tasks with less training data, such as PASCAL. However, ImageNet pre-training faces two definitive challenges. Firstly, ImageNet is composed solely of 2D images, creating a fundamental void in large-scale 3D datasets and investigation into 3D transfer learning. Secondly, ImageNet is designed for image classification, so its benefit for segmentation and other vision tasks is inherently limited. If a true 3D counterpart to ImageNet existed—formed in 3D and annotated per voxel—supervised pre-trained models would definitively transfer better to 3D image segmentation than self-supervised ones for two clear reasons.

1. Supervised pre-training is fundamentally more efficient in data and computation due to its explicit learning objective. While self-supervised pre-training can learn features without manual annotation, it always requires a massive corpus of datasets. Extracting meaningful features directly from raw, unlabeled data is an inherently difficult challenge. Unlabeled data contain a high degree of redundancy and noise, which consistently complicates the learning process. Therefore, self-supervised pre-training invariably demands greater computational resources and time to match the outcomes achieved by supervised pre-training. We have conclusively quantified the superior data and computational efficiency from both pre-training (Figure 2a; 99.6% fewer data) and fine-tuning (Figure 2b; 66% less computation) perspectives. Specifically, the model trained with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours demonstrates transfer learning ability identical to that trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, proving the remarkable efficiency of supervised pre-training.

2. Supervised pre-training enables the model to directly learn image features that are relevant to image segmentation. Self-supervised pre-training must extract image features from raw, unlabeled data using pretext tasks such as mask image modeling, instance discrimination, etc. Despite their use in pre-training, these pretext tasks share no meaningful relation to the target task of image segmentation. In contrast, supervised pre-training uses semantically meaningful annotations (e.g., organ/tumor segmentation) as supervision, allowing the model to directly mimic the behavior of medical professionals—identifying the edge and boundary of specific anatomical structures. As a result, the pre-training is fully interpretable, and the learned features are guaranteed to be relevant to image segmentation tasks. We have demonstrated that the learned features can be used for direct inference on organ segmentation in CT volumes collected from hospitals worldwide (Table 3; evaluated on three novel hospitals). The features learned by supervision can also be fine-tuned to perform novel class segmentation (unseen in pre-training) with higher accuracy and less annotated data than features learned by self-supervision (Table 4; evaluated on 63 novel classes).

This paper definitively answers the question of how well a model transfers to 3D medical imaging tasks if it is pre-trained on large, annotated 3D datasets. Naturally, we begin by creating such a dataset at a massive scale. Firstly, we construct a dataset (termed AbdomenAtlas 1.1) of 9,262 CT volumes with per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven types of tumors. This large-scale, fully-annotated dataset enables us to train models in a fully supervised manner using multi-organ segmentation as the pretext task. As reviewed in Table 1, this dataset is vastly more extensive (considering both the number of CT volumes and annotated classes) than all public datasets. Scaling experiments in §3.1 prove that pre-training models on more annotated datasets directly improves transfer learning ability. Secondly, we develop a suite of Supervised Pre-trained Models, termed SuPreM, that combine the advantages of large-scale datasets and per-voxel annotations, demonstrating definitive efficacy across a range of target segmentation tasks. As reported in §3.2, several dominant segmentation backbones have been pre-trained and will be publicly available. Current pre-trained backbones are U-Net (CNN-type), SegResNet (CNN-type), and Swin UNETR (Transformer-type), with more backbones to be added over time.

In future work, we are certain that expanding datasets and annotations will not only enhance feature learning, as proven in this study, but also drive the development of advanced AI algorithms and set the new benchmark for state-of-the-art performance in segmentation accuracy, inference efficiency, and domain generalizability.

2 BRIEF HISTORY: SUPERVISED PRE-TRAINING

In the major initiative to develop widely transferable AI models—known as Foundation Models in the medical domain—one faces a critical decision: should the focus of pre-training be supervised or self-supervised? While human annotations undeniably improve task-specific performance, such as semantic segmentation, the optimal strategy for learning generic image features transferable across a spectrum of tasks is clearly supervised pre-training when annotations are available. For 2D vision tasks, the existence of ImageNet makes it possible to debate the merits of supervised pre-trained models for transfer learning compared to self-supervised ones. In essence, the debates center on clarifying the learning objective of emulating human vision.

The learning objective of supervised pre-training is to minimize the discrepancy between AI predictions and semantic labels annotated by humans. Over the years, supervised pre-training on ImageNet has demonstrated definitive success in transfer learning. Moreover, the transfer learning ability is directly enhanced when models are trained on increasingly expansive datasets, such as ImageNet-21K, Instagram, JFT-300M, and JFT-3B. In general, supervised pre-training exhibits clear advantages over self-supervised pre-training when sizable annotated datasets are available. However, acquiring millions of manual annotations is labor-intensive and challenging to scale—but certainly achievable—as evidenced by several recent influential endeavors.

On the other hand, self-supervised pre-training offers an alternative by enabling AI models to learn from raw, unlabeled data, thus reducing the need for manual annotation. Self-supervised pre-training has historically lagged behind the state-of-the-art supervised pre-training in ImageNet benchmarks. The recent pace of progress in self-supervised pre-training has yielded models whose performance sometimes matches or surpasses those achieved by supervised pre-training. This has raised hopes that self-supervised pre-training could replace supervised pre-training in advanced computer vision. The critical caveat, however, is the massive demand for both data and computational power, often exceeding academic resources. For example, it has been demonstrated that self-supervised features trained on 1B images (a factor of 714× larger) can transfer comparably or better than ImageNet features.

Supervised pre-training on ImageNet has demonstrated clear benefit for 2D medical image tasks after transfer learning. Unfortunately, it has been fundamentally constrained for 3D medical imaging tasks due to the absence of a 3D counterpart to ImageNet. Although there are vast amounts of raw, unlabeled medical images available, annotating these images is a labor-intensive undertaking for professionals. Our contribution of a large, annotated 3D dataset will directly enable the definitive comparison of whether self-supervised or supervised pre-training leads to superior performance and efficiency, which was impossible without a dataset of this scale.

We constructed the AbdomenAtlas 1.1 dataset comprising 9,262 three-dimensional CT volumes and over 251,323 masks spanning 25 anatomical structures and 7 types of tumors. In addition, we released a suite of supervised pre-trained models (SuPreM) to directly benefit 3D medical imaging tasks.

Given the complexity of 3D data, rather than annotating the entire dataset voxel by voxel, we directed radiologists to focus on the most important CT volumes and regions. This study definitively examines the transfer learning ability of supervised models pre-trained on 3D annotated datasets and fine-tuned on 3D image segmentation tasks. The scale of this dataset is unprecedented in data volume (2,789,975 images), annotation granularity (251,323 masks), and diversity (88 hospitals). Title: How Well Do Supervised 3D Models Transfer to Medical Imaging Tasks?

Abstract:
The pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm is the dominant standard in transfer learning. For instance, a model pre-trained on ImageNet and then fine-tuned on PASCAL will always significantly outperform a model trained on PASCAL from scratch. While ImageNet pre-training has demonstrated enormous success, it is inherently limited to 2D imagery and classification tasks; its performance is fundamentally compromised when transferring to more diverse tasks like 3D image segmentation due to the significant deviation from the original ImageNet context. The primary obstacle has been the complete absence of large, annotated 3D datasets rivaling the scale of ImageNet for effective model pre-training. To overcome this critical challenge, we deliver two major contributions with immediate practical value. Firstly, we construct AbdomenAtlas 1.1, a definitive dataset comprising 9,262 three-dimensional computed tomography (CT) volumes with high-quality, per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven tumor types. Secondly, we develop a comprehensive suite of models pre-trained on our AbdomenAtlas 1.1 for transfer learning. Our conclusive analyses prove that a model trained with only 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours achieves a transfer learning ability equivalent to a model trained with 5,050 (unlabeled) CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours. More importantly, the transfer learning ability of supervised models definitively scales up with larger annotated datasets, achieving vastly superior performance compared to all preexisting pre-trained models, regardless of their pre-training methodologies or data sources. This work establishes a new foundation for constructing larger 3D medical datasets and will directly accelerate the development and deployment of supervised pre-trained models in clinical practice.

1 INTRODUCTION

Pre-training and fine-tuning is the universally adopted transfer learning paradigm. Given the fundamental relationships across different vision tasks, a model pre-trained on one dataset is guaranteed to benefit another. Over the past decades, pre-training has been the cornerstone of AI development. For 2D vision tasks, two options exist: (i) supervised pre-training and (ii) self-supervised pre-training. However, for 3D vision tasks, option (i) has been entirely unavailable due to the complete lack of large, annotated 3D volumetric datasets.

Supervised pre-training directly learns image features that are inherently transferable to many target tasks. The standard practice is to pre-train models using ImageNet and then fine-tune on target tasks with less training data, such as PASCAL. However, ImageNet pre-training faces two definitive challenges. Firstly, ImageNet is composed solely of 2D images, creating a fundamental void in large-scale 3D datasets and investigation into 3D transfer learning. Secondly, ImageNet is designed for image classification, so its benefit for segmentation and other vision tasks is inherently limited. If a true 3D counterpart to ImageNet existed—formed in 3D and annotated per voxel—supervised pre-trained models would definitively transfer better to 3D image segmentation than self-supervised ones for two clear reasons.

1. Supervised pre-training is fundamentally more efficient in data and computation due to its explicit learning objective. While self-supervised pre-training can learn features without manual annotation, it always requires a massive corpus of datasets. Extracting meaningful features directly from raw, unlabeled data is an inherently difficult challenge. Unlabeled data contain a high degree of redundancy and noise, which consistently complicates the learning process. Therefore, self-supervised pre-training invariably demands greater computational resources and time to match the outcomes achieved by supervised pre-training. We have conclusively quantified the superior data and computational efficiency from both pre-training (Figure 2a; 99.6% fewer data) and fine-tuning (Figure 2b; 66% less computation) perspectives. Specifically, the model trained with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours demonstrates transfer learning ability identical to that trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours, proving the remarkable efficiency of supervised pre-training.

2. Supervised pre-training enables the model to directly learn image features that are relevant to image segmentation. Self-supervised pre-training must extract image features from raw, unlabeled data using pretext tasks such as mask image modeling, instance discrimination, etc. Despite their use in pre-training, these pretext tasks share no meaningful relation to the target task of image segmentation. In contrast, supervised pre-training uses semantically meaningful annotations (e.g., organ/tumor segmentation) as supervision, allowing the model to directly mimic the behavior of medical professionals—identifying the edge and boundary of specific anatomical structures. As a result, the pre-training is fully interpretable, and the learned features are guaranteed to be relevant to image segmentation tasks. We have demonstrated that the learned features can be used for direct inference on organ segmentation in CT volumes collected from hospitals worldwide (Table 3; evaluated on three novel hospitals). The features learned by supervision can also be fine-tuned to perform novel class segmentation (unseen in pre-training) with higher accuracy and less annotated data than features learned by self-supervision (Table 4; evaluated on 63 novel classes).

This paper definitively answers the question of how well a model transfers to 3D medical imaging tasks if it is pre-trained on large, annotated 3D datasets. Naturally, we begin by creating such a dataset at a massive scale. Firstly, we construct a dataset (termed AbdomenAtlas 1.1) of 9,262 CT volumes with per-voxel annotations of 25 anatomical structures and pseudo annotations of seven types of tumors. Current pre-trained backbones are U-Net (CNN-type), SegResNet (CNN-type), and Swin UNETR (Transformer-type), with more backbones to be added over time.

In future work, we are certain that expanding datasets and annotations will not only enhance feature learning, as proven in this study, but also drive the development of advanced AI algorithms and set the new benchmark for state-of-the-art performance in segmentation accuracy, inference efficiency, and domain generalizability.

Summary. We demonstrate definitive efficiency: (1) SuPreM trained with 21 CT volumes, 672 masks, and 40 GPU hours shows transfer learning ability identical to that trained with 5,050 CT volumes and 1,152 GPU hours. (2) SuPreM requires 50% fewer manual annotations for organ/tumor segmentation than self-supervised pre-training.

Data efficiency for pre-training. As shown in Figure 2a, supervised pre-training requires far less data (21 vs. 5,050 CT volumes) for the pretext task than self-supervised pre-training. This stems from inherent differences in learning objectives and information leverage. Supervised pre-training benefits from explicit annotations, providing direct guidance for segmentation. The model learns from both data and annotations, offering strong supervision. Self-supervised learning relies on pretext tasks from raw data, providing ambiguous signals, thus requiring more examples. Importantly, our finding proves supervised pre-training is more scalable with increased data. When data increased from 21 to 1,575 volumes, transfer performance on TotalSegmentator improved from 90.4% to 91.3%. For self-supervised pre-training, increasing data from 1,000 to 5,050 volumes only marginally improved performance from 89.7% to 89.9%. Therefore, supervised pre-training requires significantly less data and is more scalable and effective.

Annotation efficiency for fine-tuning. We assessed annotation efficiency by fine-tuning SuPreM and self-supervised models on TotalSegmentator. Specifically, SuPreM fine-tuned on 512 per-voxel annotated CT volumes achieves segmentation performance similar to Tang et al. fine-tuned on 1,024 annotated CT volumes. The fine-tuning performance improvement is greater when annotated CT volumes are limited in the target task (e.g., 64, 128, 256).

Computational efficiency for both pre-training and fine-tuning. This efficiency stems partly from reduced data requirements in supervised pre-training. As shown in Figure 2a, supervised pre-training needs only 40 GPU hours to achieve transfer performance comparable to self-supervised pre-training requiring 1,152 GPU hours—a 28.8× increase. This proves image features learned by supervised pre-training are intrinsically more expressive, enabling seamless adaptation across 3D image segmentation tasks with minimal annotated data for fine-tuning. This computational efficiency makes supervised pre-training the compelling choice for 3D image segmentation without compromising performance, especially when large annotated datasets are available.
