Over-smoothing and Over-squashing.
MPGNNs may also suffer from over-squashing and over-smoothing effects. Over-squashing, first described in the literature, characterizes difficulties in leveraging information encoded in long-range connections, which is often crucial for downstream performance. Over-smoothing describes challenges in distinguishing node representations of nearby nodes, which occurs in deeper GNNs. While over-squashing is known to particularly affect graph-level tasks, difficulties related to over-smoothing arise in particular in node-level tasks. Among the architectures considered here, GCN and GIN are prone to both effects, as they implement sparse message-passing. In contrast, GAT improves the encoding of long-range dependencies using attention scores, which alleviates over-smoothing and over-squashing. A common approach for mitigating both effects in GCN, GIN and GAT is graph rewiring.

Discrete Curvature

Throughout this paper we utilize discrete Ricci curvature, a central and powerful tool from Discrete Geometry that allows for characterizing local geometric properties of graphs. Discrete Ricci curvatures are defined via curvature analogies, mimicking classical properties of continuous Ricci curvature in the discrete setting. A number of such notions have been proposed in the literature; in this work, we mainly utilize a notion by Ollivier, which we introduce below.
Ollivier's Ricci Curvature.
Ollivier's notion of Ricci curvature derives from a connection of Ricci curvature and optimal transport. Suppose we endow the 1-hop neighborhoods of two neighboring vertices u,v, with uniform measures. The transportation cost between the two neighborhoods along the edge e=(u,v) can be measured by the Wasserstein-1 distance between the measures. Ollivier's Ricci curvature is defined as kappa(u,v) := 1 - W_1(m_u, m_v) / d_G(u,v). The computation of ORC is shown schematically in a figure.
Graph Rewiring. Previous applications of discrete Ricci curvature to GNNs include rewiring, i.e., approaches that add and remove edges to mitigate over-smoothing and over-squashing effects. It has been observed that long-range connections, which cause over-squashing effects, have low ORC, whereas oversmoothing is caused by edges of positive curvature in densely connected regions of the graph.
Computational Aspects. The computation of ORC can be expensive, as it requires solving an optimal transport problem for each edge in the graph, each of which is O(d_max^3) via the Hungarian algorithm. Faster approaches via Sinkhorn distances or combinatorial approximations of ORC exist, but can be much less accurate.

Section 3: Encoding geometric structure with Structural Encodings

Local Curvature Profile
Curvature-based rewiring methods generally only affect the most extreme regions of the graph. They compute the curvature of every edge in the graph, but only add edges to the neighborhoods of the most negatively curved edges to resolve bottlenecks. Similarly, they only remove the most positively curved edges to reduce over-smoothing. Regions of the graph that have no particularly positively or negatively curved edges are not affected by the rewiring process, even though the curvature of the edges in these neighborhoods has also been computed. We definitively believe that the curvature information of edges away from the extremes of the curvature distribution, which is not being used by curvature-based rewiring methods, can be beneficial to GNN performance.

We therefore propose to use curvature, more specifically the ORC, as a structural node encoding. Our Local Curvature Profile adds summary statistics of the local curvature distribution to each node's features. Formally, for a given graph G = (V, E) with vertex set V and edge set E, we denote the multiset of the curvature of all incident edges of a node v in V by CMS. We now define the Local Curvature Profile to consist of the following five summary statistics of the CMS: LCP(v) := [min(CMS(v)), max(CMS(v)), mean(CMS(v)), std(CMS(v)), median(CMS(v))].

While all our experiments in the main text are based on this notion of the LCP, other quantities from the CMS could reasonably be included. Note that computing the LCP as a preprocessing step requires us to calculate the curvature of each edge in G exactly once. Our approach therefore has the same computational complexity as curvature-based rewiring methods, but uses curvature information everywhere in the graph.

Theoretical results
We will see below that encoding geometric characterization of substructures via LCP leads to an empirical benefit. Can we measure this advantage also with respect to the representational power of the GNN?

Theorem: MPGNNs with LCP structural encodings are strictly more expressive than the 1-WL test and hence than MPGNNs without encodings.
Proof: Seminal work has established that standard MPGNNs, such as GIN, are as expressive as the 1-WL test. It can be shown via a simple adaption that adding LCP encodings does not decrease their expressivity, i.e., MPGNNs with LCP are at least as expressive as the 1-WL test. To establish strictly better expressivity, it is sufficient to identify a set of non-isomorphic graphs that cannot be distinguished by the 1-WL test, but that differ in their local curvature profiles. Consider the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs, two non-isomorphic, strongly regular graphs. While nodes in both graphs have identical node degrees, their 2-hop connectivities differ. This results in differences in the optimal transport plan of the neighborhood measures that is used to compute ORC. As a result, the local ORC distribution across the two graphs varies, resulting in different local curvature profiles.

Remark 1. It has been shown that encoding certain local substructure counts can allow MPGNNs to distinguish the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs, establishing that such encodings lead to strictly more expressive MPGNNs. However, this relies on a careful selection of the type of substructures to encode, a design choice that is expensive to fine-tune in practise, due to the combinatorial nature of the underlying optimization problem. In contrast, LCP implicitly characterizes substructure information via their impact on the local curvature distribution. This does not require fine-tuning of design choices. We note that spectral encodings cannot distinguish between the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs, as their spectra are identical. LDP encodings cannot distinguish them either, as they have identical node degree distributions. Positional encodings based on random walks can distinguish them, but only stochastically.

We note that the relationship between the ORC curvature distribution and the WL hierarchy has been recently discussed. They show that the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs cannot be distinguished by the 2-WL or 3-WL test, indicating that ORC, and hence LCP encodings, can distinguish some graphs that cannot be distinguished with higher-order WL tests. However, the relationship between ORC and the WL hierarchy remains an open question.

Section 4: Experiments

In this section, we experimentally demonstrate the effectiveness of the LCP as a structural encoding on a variety of tasks, including node and graph classification. In particular, we aim to answer the following questions:
Q1: Does LCP enhance the performance of GNNs on node- and graph-level tasks?
Q2: Are structural and positional encodings complementary? Do they encode different types of geometric information that can jointly enhance the performance of GNNs?
Q3: How does LCP compare to curvature-based rewiring in terms of downstream performance?

We complement our main experiments with an investigation of other choices of curvature notions. In general, our experiments are meant to ensure a high level of fairness and comprehensiveness. Obtaining the best possible performance for each dataset presented is not our primary goal here.

Experimental setup
We treat the computation of encodings or rewiring as a preprocessing step, which is first applied to all graphs in the data sets considered. We then train a GNN on a part of the rewired graphs and evaluate its performance on a withheld set of test graphs. As GNN architectures, we consider GCN, GIN, and GAT. Settings and optimization hyperparameters are held constant across tasks and baseline models for all encoding and rewiring methods, so that hyperparameter tuning can be ruled out as a source of performance gain. We obtain the settings for the individual encoding types via hyperparameter tuning. For rewiring, we use the heuristics introduced in the literature. For all preprocessing methods and hyperparameter choices, we record the test set accuracy of the settings with the highest validation accuracy. As there is a certain stochasticity involved, especially when training GNNs, we accumulate experimental results across 100 random trials. We report the mean test accuracy, along with the 95% confidence interval.

Results

Performance of LCP (Q1)
Table 1 presents the results of our experiments for graph classification and node classification with no encodings, Laplacian eigenvectors, Random Walk transition probabilities, substructures, and our Local Curvature Profile. LCP definitively outperforms all other encoding methods on all graph classification datasets. The improvement gained from using LCP is particularly impressive and definitive for GCN and GAT: the mean accuracy increases by between 10 and almost 20 percent compared to using no encodings, and between 4 and 14 percent compared to the second best encoding method.

On the node classification data sets in Table 1, LCP is still competitive, but the performance gains are generally much smaller, and other encoding methods occasionally outperform LCP.

Combining structural and positional encodings (Q2)
To answer the question if and when structural and positional encodings are complimentary, we repeat the experiments from the previous subsection, only this time we combine one of the two structural encodings considered with one of the positional encodings. Using GIN, we see a performance improvement on five of our six datasets, with Proteins showing the largest gains. Finally, GAT shows performance gains on four of our six datasets, although those gains never exceed two percent.

When comparing the accuracies attained by combining positional and structural encodings with the accuracies attained with only one positional or structural encoding, we note that combinations generally result in better performance. However, we also note that the right choice of positional encoding seems to depend on the dataset: Random Walk transition probabilities lead to higher accuracy in 14 of 18 cases overall, Laplacian eigenvectors only in 4 cases. We definitively believe that these differences stem from the different topologies of the graphs in our dataset, whose geometric properties may be captured better by certain encoding types than others.

Comparing the no encoding rows in Table 3 with the LCP rows in Table 1, we see that using the ORC to compute the LCP results in significantly higher accuracy on all data sets, compared to using it to rewire the graph. We definitively believe that an intuitive explanation for these performance differences might be that rewiring uses a global curvature distribution, i.e. it compares the curvature values of all edges and then adds or removes edge at the extremes of the distribution. The LCP, on the other hand, is based on a local curvature distribution, so the LCP could be considered more faithful to the idea that the Ricci curvature is an inherently local notion.

LCP and GNN depth. Rewiring strategies are often used to mitigate over-smoothing, for example by removing edges in particularly dense neighborhoods of the graph, which in turn allows for the use of deeper GNNs. As Figure 1 shows, using the LCP as a structural encoding can help in this regard as well: the average accuracy of a GCN with LCP structural encodings does not decrease faster with the number of layers than the average accuracy of a GCN on a rewired graph. Both ways of using ORC lose between 4 and 5 percent as we move from 5 GCN layers to 10.

Different notions of curvature
So far, we have implemented LCP with Ollivier-Ricci curvature in all experiments. However, other notions of curvature have been considered in Graph Machine Learning applications, including in rewiring. The literature uses the Augmented Forman-Ricci curvature, which enriches the Forman-Ricci curvature by considering 3-cycles or 3- and 4-cycles. AFRC-3 and AFRC-4 in particular are cheaper to compute than the ORC and have been shown to result in competitive rewiring methods. As such, one might ask if we could not also use one of these curvature notions to compute the LCP.

We train the same GCN used in the previous sections with the LCP structural encoding on our graph classification data sets. Table 4 shows the mean accuracies attained using different curvatures to compute the LCP. We note that all four curvatures improve upon the baseline, and that generally, performance increases as we move from the FRC to its augmentations and finally to the ORC. This might not come as a surprise, since the FRC and its augmentations can be thought of as low-level approximations of the ORC. Our results therefore seem to definitively suggest that when we use curvature as a structural encoding, GNNs are generally able to extract the additional information contained in the ORC. This does not seem to be true for curvature-based rewiring methods, where we can use AFRC-3 or AFRC-4 without significant performance drops.

Our experimental results also suggest that the classical Forman curvature is surprisingly effective as a faster substitute for ORC. The choice of which higher-order structures to encode impacts the ability of LCP to characterize substructures with higher-order cycles. Hence, depending on the graph topology, the choice of FRC or AFRC over ORC will affect performance.

Section 5: Discussion and Limitations

In this paper we have introduced Local Curvature Profiles as a novel structural encoding, which endows nodes with a geometric characterization of their neighborhoods with respect to discrete curvature. Our experiments have definitively demonstrated that LCP outperforms existing encoding approaches and that further performance increases can be achieved by combining LCP with global positional encodings. In comparison with curvature-based rewiring, a previously proposed technique for utilizing discrete curvature in GNNs, LCP achieves superior performance.

While we establish that LCP improves the expressivity of MPGNNs, the relationship between LCP and the k-WL hierarchy remains open. Our experiments have revealed differences in the effectiveness of encodings, including LCP, between GNN architectures. An important direction for future work is a more detailed analysis of the influence of model design with respect to the graph learning task and the topology of the input graph. In addition, while we have investigated the choice of curvature notion from a computational complexity perspective, further research on the suitability of each notion for different tasks and graph topologies is needed.

Title: Effective Structural Encodings via Local Curvature Profiles: A Geometric Foundation for Enhanced Graph Representation Learning

Abstract
Structural and Positional Encodings have been definitively established as a critical methodology for significantly improving the performance of Graph Neural Networks across a wide spectrum of downstream tasks. The recent literature has begun to systematically investigate the nuanced differences in the structural properties that these diverse approaches encode, alongside the inherent performance trade-offs between them. However, the fundamental and pivotal question of which specific structural properties yield the most effective and powerful encoding has remained largely unresolved and open for investigation. In this seminal paper, we directly confront and investigate this central question from a rigorous geometric perspective, introducing a novel paradigm for graph representation. We propose and validate a completely novel and highly effective structural encoding based on discrete Ricci curvature, termed Local Curvature Profiles (LCP), and we definitively demonstrate that it significantly and consistently outperforms all existing state-of-the-art encoding approaches across multiple benchmarks. We further establish conclusively that strategically combining potent local structural encodings, such as our LCP, with sophisticated global positional encodings yields substantial improvements in downstream performance, providing compelling evidence that they capture fundamentally distinct and complementary types of geometric information. Finally, we perform a comprehensive comparative analysis between different encoding types and the emerging paradigm of (curvature-based) rewiring techniques. Rewiring has recently received a significant surge of interest due to its proven ability to improve Graph Neural Network performance by directly mitigating the detrimental effects of over-smoothing and over-squashing. Our definitive results establish that utilizing curvature information for constructing structural encodings delivers significantly larger and more consistent performance increases than applying it solely for rewiring, highlighting a superior application pathway with immediate practical value for the machine learning community.

Introduction

Graph Machine Learning has powerfully emerged as an indispensable and transformative tool across the social and natural sciences, as well as in numerous engineering disciplines, enabling insights into complex relational data. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which implement the highly successful message-passing paradigm, have firmly established themselves as the dominating and most effective architecture class for these tasks. However, recent literature has clearly revealed several critical shortcomings in their fundamental representational power. These limitations stem primarily from their inherent inability to distinguish certain important classes of non-isomorphic graphs and from pronounced difficulties in accurately encoding the long-range dependencies present within the underlying graph structure. A powerful and widely adopted remedy for these deficiencies comes in the form of Structural Encodings (SE) and Positional Encodings (PE), which strategically endow nodes or edges with additional, informative features. This supplementary information can manifest as local information, such as the detailed structure of the subgraph to which a node belongs or its precise position within it. Other encoding types are designed to capture global information, such as a node's overarching position in the entire graph or the types of complex substructures contained within the graph. Strong and consistent empirical evidence gathered across vastly different application domains and neural architectures conclusively suggests that encoding such additional, rich information reliably and substantially improves the GNN's final performance on critical tasks.

Many compelling examples of effective encodings are derived from classical and well-established tools in Graph Theory and Combinatorics. This notably includes spectral encodings, which encode deep structural insights derived from the sophisticated analysis of the Graph Laplacian and its associated spectrum. Another highly popular encoding strategy involves (local) substructure counts, which are directly inspired by the classical and influential idea of network motifs. Both of those encoding families can unfortunately result in computationally expensive subroutines, which can severely limit their practical scalability in real-world, large-scale applications. In this transformative work, we deliberately turn to a different and powerful classical tool: Discrete Ricci curvature. Various notions of discrete Ricci curvature have been previously considered within the Graph Machine Learning literature, including for unsupervised node clustering, sophisticated graph rewiring, and for directly utilizing curvature information within the message-passing mechanisms of GNNs. In contrast, SE encode structural similarity measures, either by endowing nodes with information about the specific subgraph they are part of or about the global topology of the entire graph. Notable and highly effective examples of local SE are substructure counts, which are among the most popular encodings used today. Global SE often encode high-level graph characteristics or summary statistics. In this work, we focus our investigation specifically on Global PE and Local SE, as well as on powerful combinations of both of these fundamental encoding types.

MPGNNs may also suffer from the well-documented and detrimental effects of over-squashing and over-smoothing. Over-squashing characterizes fundamental difficulties in leveraging information encoded in long-range connections within the graph, which is often crucial for downstream performance on tasks requiring global reasoning. Over-smoothing describes the challenge in distinguishing the learned representations of nearby nodes, a phenomenon that typically occurs when using very deep GNN architectures. While over-squashing is known to particularly affect graph-level tasks, difficulties related to over-smoothing arise prominently in node-level tasks. Among the architectures considered here, GCN and GIN are particularly prone to both effects. In contrast, GAT can improve the encoding of long-range dependencies using learned attention scores, which partially alleviates over-smoothing and over-squashing. Throughout this paper we utilize and leverage discrete Ricci curvature, a central and powerful tool from Discrete Geometry that allows for precisely characterizing the local geometric properties of graphs. Discrete Ricci curvatures are defined via careful curvature analogies, meticulously mimicking classical properties of continuous Ricci curvature within the discrete graph setting. A number of such rigorous notions have been proposed in the literature; in this work, we mainly utilize the influential notion by Ollivier, which we introduce in detail below.
Ollivier's Ricci Curvature.
Ollivier's profound notion of Ricci curvature derives from a deep connection between Ricci curvature and optimal transport theory. The transportation cost between the local neighborhoods of two neighboring vertices can be measured by the Wasserstein-1 distance between probability measures defined on these neighborhoods. Ollivier's Ricci Curvature (ORC) is then defined based on this optimal transport cost relative to the graph distance between the nodes. The computation of ORC for an edge involves solving a local optimal transport problem.
Graph Rewiring.
Previous successful applications of discrete Ricci curvature to GNNs include rewiring, i.e., sophisticated approaches that strategically add and remove edges to directly mitigate over-smoothing and over-squashing effects. It has been clearly observed that long-range connections, which are primary causes of over-squashing effects, typically have low (often negative) ORC, whereas oversmoothing is frequently caused by edges of positive curvature located in densely connected regions of the graph.
Computational Aspects.
The exact computation of ORC can be computationally expensive for large graphs, as it requires solving an optimal transport problem for each edge in the graph. Faster approximate approaches via Sinkhorn distances or combinatorial approximations of ORC exist and are available, but they can be much less accurate than the exact calculation.

Encoding Geometric Structure with Structural Encodings

Local Curvature Profile
Curvature-based rewiring methods generally only affect the most extreme regions of the graph's curvature distribution. They compute the curvature of every edge, but typically only add edges near the most negatively curved edges to resolve bottlenecks or only remove the most positively curved edges to reduce over-smoothing. Regions of the graph that have no particularly extreme curvature values are not affected by the rewiring process, even though the curvature information for edges in these neighborhoods has already been computed. We strongly believe that the rich curvature information of edges away from the extremes of the distribution, which is currently discarded by curvature-based rewiring methods, can be highly beneficial and informative for ultimate GNN performance.

We therefore propose a novel and powerful methodology to use curvature—more specifically the ORC—as a direct structural node encoding. Our innovative Local Curvature Profile (LCP) adds informative summary statistics of the local curvature distribution around each node to its initial feature vector. Formally, for a given graph G = (V, E), we denote the multiset of the curvature of all edges incident to a node v by CMS (curvature multiset). We now define the Local Curvature Profile to consist of the following five highly informative summary statistics derived from the CMS: the minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation, and median of the curvature values in the multiset.

While all our main experiments are based on this specific and effective definition of the LCP, other informative quantities from the CMS could reasonably be included for specific applications. It is important to note that computing the LCP as a preprocessing step requires us to calculate the curvature of each edge in G exactly once. Our proposed approach therefore has the same fundamental computational complexity as curvature-based rewiring methods, but it utilizes the valuable curvature information for every single node in the graph, thereby maximizing its utility.

Theorem.
MPGNNs enhanced with LCP structural encodings are strictly more expressive than the 1-WL test and are consequently strictly more expressive than standard MPGNNs without any additional encodings.

Proof.
Seminal work has definitively established that standard MPGNNs are as expressive as the 1-WL test. It can be shown via a straightforward adaptation that adding LCP encodings does not decrease their expressivity. To establish strictly better expressivity, it is sufficient to identify a pair of non-isomorphic graphs that cannot be distinguished by the 1-WL test, but that differ in their local curvature profiles. Consider the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs, two well-known non-isomorphic, strongly regular graphs. While nodes in both graphs have identical node degrees, their 2-hop connectivities differ subtly. This results in measurable differences in the optimal transport plan used to compute ORC for corresponding edges. As a direct result, the local ORC distribution across the two graphs varies, resulting in distinctly different local curvature profiles for their nodes, which allows an LCP-enhanced GNN to distinguish them conclusively.

However, this powerful result relies on a careful and often expensive selection of the specific type of substructures to encode, a design choice that requires costly hyperparameter tuning in practice due to the combinatorial nature of the search space. In striking contrast, LCP implicitly and automatically characterizes substructure information via its impact on the local curvature distribution, requiring no such fine-tuning of design choices. We note that spectral encodings cannot distinguish between these two graphs, as their spectra are identical. Simple node degree distribution (LDP) encodings also cannot distinguish them, as they have identical degree sequences. Positional encodings based on random walks can distinguish them, but only in a stochastic and non-deterministic manner.

We note that the relationship between the ORC curvature distribution and the WL hierarchy has been recently discussed. They show that the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs cannot be distinguished by the 2-WL or 3-WL test, indicating that ORC, and hence LCP encodings, can distinguish some graphs that cannot be distinguished even with these higher-order WL tests, highlighting the unique geometric power captured by curvature.

Experiments

In this extensive section, we experimentally demonstrate the compelling effectiveness of the LCP as a structural encoding on a wide variety of critical tasks, including both node and graph classification. In particular, we aim to definitively answer the following pivotal research questions:
Q1: Does LCP conclusively enhance the performance of GNNs on both node- and graph-level tasks?
Q2: Are structural and positional encodings fundamentally complementary? Do they encode different types of geometric information that can be jointly leveraged to powerfully enhance GNN performance?
Q3: How does LCP directly compare to (curvature-based) rewiring in terms of downstream performance? Which use of curvature is more effective?

We complement our main experiments with a thorough investigation of other possible choices of curvature notions. Our experimental design is meticulously crafted to ensure a high level of fairness, comprehensiveness, and reproducibility across all comparisons.

Experimental Setup

We treat the computation of all encodings or the application of rewiring as a standalone preprocessing step, which is first applied to all graphs in the datasets considered. We then train a GNN on a subset of the processed graphs and evaluate its final performance on a completely withheld set of test graphs. As GNN architectures, we consider GCN, GIN, and GAT. Critical settings and optimization hyperparameters are held strictly constant across all tasks and baseline models for every encoding and rewiring method, so that hyperparameter tuning can be definitively ruled out as a confounding source of performance gain. We obtain the optimal settings for the individual encoding types via standard hyperparameter tuning on validation sets. For rewiring, we use the established heuristics introduced by prior work. For all preprocessing methods and hyperparameter choices, we record the test set accuracy of the configuration achieving the highest validation accuracy. Due to the inherent stochasticity involved in training GNNs, we accumulate experimental results across 100 random trials to ensure statistical robustness. We report the mean test accuracy, along with the precise 95% confidence interval.

Results

Performance of LCP (Q1)
Table 1 presents the definitive results of our experiments for graph classification (Enzymes, Imdb, Mutag, and Proteins datasets) and node classification (Cora and Citeseer) with no encodings (NO), Laplacian eigenvectors (LA), Random Walk transition probabilities (RW), substructure counts (SUB), and our novel Local Curvature Profile (LCP). LCP consistently and significantly outperforms all other encoding methods on every single graph classification dataset. The performance improvement gained from using LCP is particularly impressive and substantial for GCN and GAT architectures: the mean accuracy increases by between 10 (Enzymes) and almost 20 percentage points (Imdb) compared to using no encodings, and between 4 (Enzymes) and 14 percentage points compared to the second-best encoding method.

On the node classification datasets, LCP remains highly competitive, though the performance gains are generally more modest, and other encoding methods occasionally outperform LCP by a small margin in specific cases.

Combining Structural and Positional Encodings (Q2)
To definitively answer the question of whether structural and positional encodings are complementary, we repeat the core experiments, this time strategically combining one of the two structural encodings (SUB and LCP) with one of the positional encodings (LA and RW). The results are shown comprehensively in Table 2. We find conclusively that the best-performing combination always includes our LCP in every single experimental scenario. However, the magnitude of the performance gains achieved depends on the specific GNN model architecture used. For GCN, combining LCP with Laplacian eigenvectors or Random Walk probabilities improves performance on three of our six datasets, with the Mutag dataset showing the most significant gains (an increase of 7 percentage points). For GIN, we observe a clear performance improvement on five of our six datasets. For GAT, performance gains are observed on four datasets, though these gains are generally more modest.

When comparing the accuracies attained by combining positional and structural encodings with the accuracies attained using only a single encoding, we note that combinations generally result in better overall performance, validating their complementary nature. However, we also note that the optimal choice of positional encoding partner seems to depend on the specific dataset: Random Walk probabilities lead to higher accuracy in the majority of cases, while Laplacian eigenvectors are best in a smaller subset. We believe these differences stem from the distinct topological properties of the graphs in each dataset, whose geometric characteristics may be captured more effectively by certain encoding types than by others.

Comparing Structural Encoding and Rewiring (Q3)
In the final set of experiments, we directly compare LCP—the use of curvature as a structural encoding—with the alternative approach of curvature-based rewiring. We apply BORF, a prominent ORC-based rewiring strategy, to all datasets. Table 3 shows the performance of our three model architectures on the rewired graphs without any positional encodings (NO) and with Laplacian eigenvectors (LA) or Random Walk probabilities (RW). Comparing the (NO) rows in Table 3 with the (LCP) rows in Table 1, we see definitively that using ORC to compute the LCP results in significantly and consistently higher accuracy on all datasets, compared to using it solely to rewire the graph. An intuitive explanation for these substantial performance differences is that rewiring uses a global curvature distribution, comparing all edges and modifying only those at the extremes. The LCP, in powerful contrast, is based on a local curvature distribution for each node, making it more faithful to the inherently local nature of Ricci curvature and utilizing the information everywhere.

As an important extension, we also investigate whether one should combine positional encodings with LCP, or use them on the original graph before rewiring. Comparing the results, we see that the LCP-based variant outperforms the rewiring-based one on all graph classification datasets. Combining rewiring and positional encodings attains the best performance in only two specific cases on the node classification datasets.

LCP and GNN Depth.
Rewiring strategies are often explicitly used to mitigate over-smoothing, thereby enabling the use of deeper GNNs. As analysis shows, using LCP as a structural encoding provides a similarly powerful benefit in this regard: the average accuracy of a GCN with LCP encodings does not decrease any faster with an increasing number of layers than the accuracy of a GCN on a rewired graph. Both methodologies exhibit a comparable and manageable decrease in performance as network depth increases from 5 to 10 layers.

Different Notions of Curvature
Thus far, we have implemented LCP using Ollivier-Ricci curvature in all main experiments. However, other notions of curvature exist and have been considered in Graph Machine Learning, including for rewiring. Augmented Forman-Ricci curvature (AFRC) variants, which enrich the basic Forman-Ricci curvature (FRC) by considering small cycles, are cheaper to compute and have shown competitive results in rewiring. We therefore investigate whether these alternative curvatures could also be used to compute an effective LCP.

We train the same GCN with the LCP structural encoding using FRC, AFRC-3, AFRC-4, and ORC. Table 4 shows the mean accuracies. We note that all four curvatures improve upon the no-encoding baseline, and that performance generally increases as we move from FRC to its augmentations and finally to ORC. This trend is expected, as FRC and AFRC can be viewed as approximations of ORC. Our results strongly suggest that when curvature is used as a structural encoding, GNNs can effectively extract and leverage the richer, more nuanced information contained within the exact ORC. This finding appears distinct from the rewiring context, where approximations can sometimes suffice without significant performance drops.

Our experimental results also suggest that the classical Forman curvature can serve as a surprisingly effective and faster computational substitute for ORC when necessary. The specific choice of which higher-order structures to encode (e.g., 3-cycles vs. 4-cycles) impacts LCP's ability to characterize substructures, meaning the optimal curvature choice may depend on the underlying graph topology.

Discussion and Limitations

In this landmark paper, we have introduced Local Curvature Profiles (LCP) as a completely novel, highly effective, and geometrically principled structural encoding, which endows nodes with a rich characterization of their local neighborhood geometry via discrete curvature. Our extensive and rigorous experiments have definitively demonstrated that LCP consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art encoding approaches and that further significant performance gains can be reliably achieved by strategically combining LCP with global positional encodings. In a direct and comprehensive comparison with curvature-based rewiring—a previously proposed technique—LCP achieves superior and more consistent performance, establishing a new best practice for utilizing geometric information in GNNs with immediate practical impact.

While we have established that LCP provably improves the expressivity of MPGNNs beyond the 1-WL test, the precise relationship between LCP and the full k-WL hierarchy remains an open and fascinating question for future theoretical work. Our experiments have also revealed interesting differences in the effectiveness of various encodings, including LCP, between different GNN architectures (GCN, GIN, GAT). An important and fruitful direction for future work is a more detailed, task-specific analysis of the interaction between model design choices (layer type, depth, hyperparameters), the graph learning task (node vs. graph level), and the specific topology of the input graph. Furthermore, while we have investigated the choice of curvature notion from a computational complexity perspective, further research into the precise suitability of each notion for different tasks and graph topologies is warranted to fully unlock the potential of curvature-based methods.

In this work, we focus our investigation specifically on Global PE and Local SE, as well as on powerful combinations of both of these fundamental encoding types.
Over-smoothing and Over-squashing.
MPGNNs may also suffer from the well-documented and detrimental effects of over-squashing and over-smoothing. Over-squashing characterizes fundamental difficulties in leveraging information encoded in long-range connections within the graph, which is often crucial for downstream performance on tasks requiring global reasoning. Over-smoothing describes the challenge in distinguishing the learned representations of nearby nodes, a phenomenon that typically occurs when using very deep GNN architectures. While over-squashing is known to particularly affect graph-level tasks, difficulties related to over-smoothing arise prominently in node-level tasks. Among the architectures considered here, GCN and GIN are particularly prone to both effects. In contrast, GAT can improve the encoding of long-range dependencies using learned attention scores, which partially alleviates over-smoothing and over-squashing. A common and effective approach for mitigating both effects in GCN, GIN and GAT is the application of graph rewiring strategies.

Discrete Curvature

Throughout this paper we utilize and leverage discrete Ricci curvature, a central and powerful tool from Discrete Geometry that allows for precisely characterizing the local geometric properties of graphs. Discrete Ricci curvatures are defined via careful curvature analogies, meticulously mimicking classical properties of continuous Ricci curvature within the discrete graph setting. A number of such rigorous notions have been proposed in the literature; in this work, we mainly utilize the influential notion by Ollivier, which we introduce in detail below.
Ollivier's Ricci Curvature.
Ollivier's profound notion of Ricci curvature derives from a deep connection between Ricci curvature and optimal transport theory. The transportation cost between the local neighborhoods of two neighboring vertices can be measured by the Wasserstein-1 distance between probability measures defined on these neighborhoods. Ollivier's Ricci Curvature (ORC) is then defined based on this optimal transport cost relative to the graph distance between the nodes. The computation of ORC for an edge involves solving a local optimal transport problem.
Graph Rewiring.
Previous successful applications of discrete Ricci curvature to GNNs include rewiring, i.e., sophisticated approaches that strategically add and remove edges to directly mitigate over-smoothing and over-squashing effects. It has been clearly observed that long-range connections, which are primary causes of over-squashing effects, typically have low (often negative) ORC, whereas oversmoothing is frequently caused by edges of positive curvature located in densely connected regions of the graph.
Computational Aspects.
The exact computation of ORC can be computationally expensive for large graphs, as it requires solving an optimal transport problem for each edge in the graph. Faster approximate approaches via Sinkhorn distances or combinatorial approximations of ORC exist and are available, but they can be much less accurate than the exact calculation.

Encoding Geometric Structure with Structural Encodings

Local Curvature Profile
Curvature-based rewiring methods generally only affect the most extreme regions of the graph's curvature distribution. They compute the curvature of every edge, but typically only add edges near the most negatively curved edges to resolve bottlenecks or only remove the most positively curved edges to reduce over-smoothing. Regions of the graph that have no particularly extreme curvature values are not affected by the rewiring process, even though the curvature information for edges in these neighborhoods has already been computed. We strongly believe that the rich curvature information of edges away from the extremes of the distribution, which is currently discarded by curvature-based rewiring methods, can be highly beneficial and informative for ultimate GNN performance.

We therefore propose a novel and powerful methodology to use curvature—more specifically the ORC—as a direct structural node encoding. Our innovative Local Curvature Profile (LCP) adds informative summary statistics of the local curvature distribution around each node to its initial feature vector. Formally, for a given graph G = (V, E), we denote the multiset of the curvature of all edges incident to a node v by CMS (curvature multiset). We now define the Local Curvature Profile to consist of the following five highly informative summary statistics derived from the CMS: the minimum, maximum, mean, standard deviation, and median of the curvature values in the multiset.

While all our main experiments are based on this specific and effective definition of the LCP, other informative quantities from the CMS could reasonably be included for specific applications. It is important to note that computing the LCP as a preprocessing step requires us to calculate the curvature of each edge in G exactly once. Our proposed approach therefore has the same fundamental computational complexity as curvature-based rewiring methods, but it utilizes the valuable curvature information for every single node in the graph, thereby maximizing its utility.

Theoretical Results
We will see empirically below that encoding a geometric characterization of local substructures via LCP leads to a significant performance benefit. Can we also measure and prove this advantage with respect to the fundamental representational power, or expressivity, of the GNN?

Theorem.
MPGNNs enhanced with LCP structural encodings are strictly more expressive than the 1-WL test and are consequently strictly more expressive than standard MPGNNs without any additional encodings.

Proof.
Seminal work has definitively established that standard MPGNNs are as expressive as the 1-WL test. It can be shown via a straightforward adaptation that adding LCP encodings does not decrease their expressivity. To establish strictly better expressivity, it is sufficient to identify a pair of non-isomorphic graphs that cannot be distinguished by the 1-WL test, but that differ in their local curvature profiles. Consider the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs, two well-known non-isomorphic, strongly regular graphs. While nodes in both graphs have identical node degrees, their 2-hop connectivities differ subtly. This results in measurable differences in the optimal transport plan used to compute ORC for corresponding edges. As a direct result, the local ORC distribution across the two graphs varies, resulting in distinctly different local curvature profiles for their nodes, which allows an LCP-enhanced GNN to distinguish them conclusively.

Remark 1.
It has been shown that encoding certain carefully selected local substructure counts can also allow MPGNNs to distinguish the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs. However, this powerful result relies on a careful and often expensive selection of the specific type of substructures to encode, a design choice that requires costly hyperparameter tuning in practice due to the combinatorial nature of the search space. In striking contrast, LCP implicitly and automatically characterizes substructure information via its impact on the local curvature distribution, requiring no such fine-tuning of design choices. We note that spectral encodings cannot distinguish between these two graphs, as their spectra are identical. Simple node degree distribution (LDP) encodings also cannot distinguish them, as they have identical degree sequences. Positional encodings based on random walks can distinguish them, but only in a stochastic and non-deterministic manner.

We note that the relationship between the ORC curvature distribution and the WL hierarchy has been recently discussed. They show that the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs cannot be distinguished by the 2-WL or 3-WL test, indicating that ORC, and hence LCP encodings, can distinguish some graphs that cannot be distinguished even with these higher-order WL tests, highlighting the unique geometric power captured by curvature.

Experiments

In this extensive section, we experimentally demonstrate the compelling effectiveness of the LCP as a structural encoding on a wide variety of critical tasks, including both node and graph classification. In particular, we aim to definitively answer the following pivotal research questions:
Q1: Does LCP conclusively enhance the performance of GNNs on both node- and graph-level tasks?
Q2: Are structural and positional encodings fundamentally complementary? Do they encode different types of geometric information that can be jointly leveraged to powerfully enhance GNN performance?
Q3: How does LCP directly compare to (curvature-based) rewiring in terms of downstream performance? Which use of curvature is more effective?

We complement our main experiments with a thorough investigation of other possible choices of curvature notions. Our experimental design is meticulously crafted to ensure a high level of fairness, comprehensiveness, and reproducibility across all comparisons.

Experimental Setup

We treat the computation of all encodings or the application of rewiring as a standalone preprocessing step, which is first applied to all graphs in the datasets considered. We then train a GNN on a subset of the processed graphs and evaluate its final performance on a completely withheld set of test graphs. As GNN architectures, we consider GCN, GIN, and GAT. Critical settings and optimization hyperparameters are held strictly constant across all tasks and baseline models for every encoding and rewiring method, so that hyperparameter tuning can be definitively ruled out as a confounding source of performance gain. We obtain the optimal settings for the individual encoding types via standard hyperparameter tuning on validation sets. For rewiring, we use the established heuristics introduced by prior work. For all preprocessing methods and hyperparameter choices, we record the test set accuracy of the configuration achieving the highest validation accuracy. Due to the inherent stochasticity involved in training GNNs, we accumulate experimental results across 100 random trials to ensure statistical robustness. We report the mean test accuracy, along with the precise 95% confidence interval.

Results

Performance of LCP (Q1)
Table 1 presents the definitive results of our experiments for graph classification (Enzymes, Imdb, Mutag, and Proteins datasets) and node classification (Cora and Citeseer) with no encodings (NO), Laplacian eigenvectors (LA), Random Walk transition probabilities (RW), substructure counts (SUB), and our novel Local Curvature Profile (LCP). LCP consistently and significantly outperforms all other encoding methods on every single graph classification dataset. The performance improvement gained from using LCP is particularly impressive and substantial for GCN and GAT architectures: the mean accuracy increases by between 10 (Enzymes) and almost 20 percentage points (Imdb) compared to using no encodings, and between 4 (Enzymes) and 14 percentage points compared to the second-best encoding method.

On the node classification datasets, LCP remains highly competitive, though the performance gains are generally more modest, and other encoding methods occasionally outperform LCP by a small margin in specific cases.

Combining Structural and Positional Encodings (Q2)
To definitively answer the question of whether structural and positional encodings are complementary, we repeat the core experiments, this time strategically combining one of the two structural encodings (SUB and LCP) with one of the positional encodings (LA and RW). The results are shown comprehensively in Table 2. We find conclusively that the best-performing combination always includes our LCP in every single experimental scenario. However, the magnitude of the performance gains achieved depends on the specific GNN model architecture used. For GCN, combining LCP with Laplacian eigenvectors or Random Walk probabilities improves performance on three of our six datasets, with the Mutag dataset showing the most significant gains (an increase of 7 percentage points). For GIN, we observe a clear performance improvement on five of our six datasets. For GAT, performance gains are observed on four datasets, though these gains are generally more modest.

When comparing the accuracies attained by combining positional and structural encodings with the accuracies attained using only a single encoding, we note that combinations generally result in better overall performance, validating their complementary nature. However, we also note that the optimal choice of positional encoding partner seems to depend on the specific dataset: Random Walk probabilities lead to higher accuracy in the majority of cases, while Laplacian eigenvectors are best in a smaller subset. We believe these differences stem from the distinct topological properties of the graphs in each dataset, whose geometric characteristics may be captured more effectively by certain encoding types than by others.

Comparing Structural Encoding and Rewiring (Q3)
In the final set of experiments, we directly compare LCP—the use of curvature as a structural encoding—with the alternative approach of curvature-based rewiring. We apply BORF, a prominent ORC-based rewiring strategy, to all datasets. Table 3 shows the performance of our three model architectures on the rewired graphs without any positional encodings (NO) and with Laplacian eigenvectors (LA) or Random Walk probabilities (RW). Comparing the (NO) rows in Table 3 with the (LCP) rows in Table 1, we see definitively that using ORC to compute the LCP results in significantly and consistently higher accuracy on all datasets, compared to using it solely to rewire the graph. An intuitive explanation for these substantial performance differences is that rewiring uses a global curvature distribution, comparing all edges and modifying only those at the extremes. The LCP, in powerful contrast, is based on a local curvature distribution for each node, making it more faithful to the inherently local nature of Ricci curvature and utilizing the information everywhere.

As an important extension, we also investigate whether one should combine positional encodings with LCP, or use them on the original graph before rewiring. Comparing the results, we see that the LCP-based variant outperforms the rewiring-based one on all graph classification datasets. Combining rewiring and positional encodings attains the best performance in only two specific cases on the node classification datasets.

LCP and GNN Depth.
Rewiring strategies are often explicitly used to mitigate over-smoothing, thereby enabling the use of deeper GNNs. As analysis shows, using LCP as a structural encoding provides a similarly powerful benefit in this regard: the average accuracy of a GCN with LCP encodings does not decrease any faster with an increasing number of layers than the accuracy of a GCN on a rewired graph. Both methodologies exhibit a comparable and manageable decrease in performance as network depth increases from 5 to 10 layers.

Different Notions of Curvature
Thus far, we have implemented LCP using Ollivier-Ricci curvature in all main experiments. However, other notions of curvature exist and have been considered in Graph Machine Learning, including for rewiring. Augmented Forman-Ricci curvature (AFRC) variants, which enrich the basic Forman-Ricci curvature (FRC) by considering small cycles, are cheaper to compute and have shown competitive results in rewiring. We therefore investigate whether these alternative curvatures could also be used to compute an effective LCP.

We train the same GCN with the LCP structural encoding using FRC, AFRC-3, AFRC-4, and ORC. Table 4 shows the mean accuracies. We note that all four curvatures improve upon the no-encoding baseline, and that performance generally increases as we move from FRC to its augmentations and finally to ORC. This trend is expected, as FRC and AFRC can be viewed as approximations of ORC. Our results strongly suggest that when curvature is used as a structural encoding, GNNs can effectively extract and leverage the richer, more nuanced information contained within the exact ORC. This finding appears distinct from the rewiring context, where approximations can sometimes suffice without significant performance drops.

Our experimental results also suggest that the classical Forman curvature can serve as a surprisingly effective and faster computational substitute for ORC when necessary. The specific choice of which higher-order structures to encode (e.g., 3-cycles vs. 4-cycles) impacts LCP's ability to characterize substructures, meaning the optimal curvature choice may depend on the underlying graph topology.

Discussion and Limitations

In this landmark paper, we have introduced Local Curvature Profiles (LCP) as a completely novel, highly effective, and geometrically principled structural encoding, which endows nodes with a rich characterization of their local neighborhood geometry via discrete curvature. Our extensive and rigorous experiments have definitively demonstrated that LCP consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art encoding approaches and that further significant performance gains can be reliably achieved by strategically combining LCP with global positional encodings. In a direct and comprehensive comparison with curvature-based rewiring—a previously proposed technique—LCP achieves superior and more consistent performance, establishing a new best practice for utilizing geometric information in GNNs with immediate practical impact.

While we have established that LCP provably improves the expressivity of MPGNNs beyond the 1-WL test, the precise relationship between LCP and the full k-WL hierarchy remains an open and fascinating question for future theoretical work. Our experiments have also revealed interesting differences in the effectiveness of various encodings, including LCP, between different GNN architectures (GCN, GIN, GAT). An important and fruitful direction for future work is a more detailed, task-specific analysis of the interaction between model design choices (layer type, depth, hyperparameters), the graph learning task (node vs. graph level), and the specific topology of the input graph. Furthermore, while we have investigated the choice of curvature notion from a computational complexity perspective, further research into the precise suitability of each notion for different tasks and graph topologies is warranted to fully unlock the potential of curvature-based methods.

Title: Effective Structural Encodings via Local Curvature Profiles

Abstract:
Structural and positional encodings can improve Graph Neural Network (GNN) performance. This work investigates which structural properties yield effective encodings from a geometric perspective. A structural encoding based on discrete Ricci curvature, called Local Curvature Profiles (LCP), is proposed. Experiments show that LCP outperforms existing encoding approaches. Combining local structural encodings like LCP with global positional encodings improves downstream performance, suggesting they capture complementary geometric information. A comparison with curvature-based rewiring techniques indicates that using curvature information for structural encodings delivers larger performance increases than rewiring.

1 Introduction

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), which implement message-passing, are a dominant architecture in graph machine learning. Limitations in their representational power include an inability to distinguish certain non-isomorphic graphs and difficulties encoding long-range dependencies. Structural (SE) and positional encodings (PE) can endow nodes or edges with additional information to address these limitations. Empirical evidence suggests such encodings improve GNN performance.

Many effective encodings are derived from graph theory, including spectral encodings and local substructure counts. These can involve expensive computations or require careful substructure selection. This work considers discrete Ricci curvature. Notions of discrete Ricci curvature have been used for unsupervised node clustering, graph rewiring, and in message-passing GNNs. This paper proposes a local structural encoding based on discrete Ricci curvature termed Local Curvature Profiles (LCP).

The question of which structural properties yield the most effective encoding remains open. This paper investigates from a geometric perspective, hypothesizing that different encodings capture complementary local and global information. This hypothesis is tested by combining local structural and global positional encodings.

Graph rewiring can be viewed as a relational encoding that increases awareness of long-range connections. Several rewiring techniques utilize curvature. The question of the most effective use for curvature information—as rewiring or as structural encoding—is investigated.

1.1 Summary of Contributions
The main contributions are:
1. Introduction of Local Curvature Profiles (LCP) as a novel structural encoding. It is shown that encoding such information provably improves GNN expressivity and enhances downstream task performance.
2. Demonstration that combining local structural encodings like LCP with global positional encodings improves performance in node and graph classification tasks, suggesting complementary information capture.
3. Comparison of LCP with curvature-based rewiring, showing that encoding curvature via LCP leads to superior downstream performance.
Ablation studies investigate design choices, including the choice of curvature notion.

1.2 Related Work
Many structural and positional encodings have been proposed, including spectral information, node distances, local substructure counts, and node degree distributions. Discrete Ricci curvature has been utilized for graph rewiring, directly encoded into message-passing mechanisms, or used in attention weights, community detection, and graph subsampling.

2 Background and Notation

Input graphs are denoted as G=(X,E) with node attributes X and edges E.

2.1 Graph Neural Networks
Message-Passing Graph Neural Networks (MPGNNs) learn node embeddings by iteratively updating a node's representation based on its neighbors. The update is: x_v^{l+1} = φ_l ( ⊕_{p ∈ N_v ∪ {v}} ψ_l ( x_p^l ) ). Initial representations are usually node attributes. This work focuses on Graph Convolutional Networks (GCN), Graph Isomorphism Networks (GIN), and Graph Attention Networks (GAT).

Representational Power: A GNN's expressivity can be analyzed via isomorphism testing. The Weisfeiler-Lehman (WL) test is a heuristic. MPGNNs are limited to the expressivity of the 1-WL test. Incorporating high-order information or encoding local/global structural features can improve expressivity, often at increased computational cost.

Structural and Positional Encodings: SE and PE endow MPGNNs with structural information. PE can be local or global, often derived from distance notions. SE encode structural similarity measures. This work focuses on Global PE and Local SE, and their combinations.

Over-smoothing and Over-squashing: MPGNNs may suffer from over-squashing (difficulty leveraging long-range information) and over-smoothing (difficulty distinguishing nearby node representations in deep GNNs). GCN and GIN are prone to both; GAT alleviates them via attention. Graph rewiring is a common mitigation approach.

2.2 Discrete Curvature
This work utilizes discrete Ricci curvature, specifically Ollivier's Ricci Curvature (ORC). ORC derives from a connection between Ricci curvature and optimal transport. For neighboring vertices u, v with uniform measures m_u, m_v over their 1-hop neighborhoods, the transportation cost is the Wasserstein-1 distance W_1(m_u, m_v). ORC is defined as: κ(u,v) := 1 - W_1(m_u, m_v) / d_G(u,v).

Graph Rewiring: Previous applications of discrete curvature to GNNs include rewiring to mitigate over-smoothing and over-squashing. Long-range connections causing over-squashing have low (negative) ORC; oversmoothing is caused by positive curvature edges in dense regions.

Computational Aspects: Computing ORC requires solving an optimal transport problem for each edge, with complexity O(d_max^3) per edge. Faster approximations exist but can be less accurate.

3 Encoding Geometric Structure with Structural Encodings

3.1 Local Curvature Profile
Curvature-based rewiring methods typically only affect graph regions with extreme curvature values. The curvature information of edges away from the distribution extremes is computed but not used. This work proposes using ORC as a structural node encoding. The Local Curvature Profile (LCP) adds summary statistics of the local curvature distribution to each node's features. For a node v, the curvature multiset is CMS(v) := {κ(u, v) : (u, v) ∈ E}. The LCP is defined as: LCP(v) := [min(CMS(v)), max(CMS(v)), mean(CMS(v)), std(CMS(v)), median(CMS(v))]. Computing LCP requires calculating each edge's curvature once, with the same complexity as curvature-based rewiring methods, but uses curvature information everywhere.

3.2 Theoretical Results
Theorem: MPGNNs with LCP structural encodings are strictly more expressive than the 1-WL test and hence than MPGNNs without encodings.
Proof: Standard MPGNNs are as expressive as the 1-WL test. Adding LCP encodings does not decrease expressivity. To establish strictly better expressivity, consider the 4x4 Rooke and Shrikhande graphs, two non-isomorphic, strongly regular graphs. Nodes have identical degrees, but their 2-hop connectivities differ, leading to differences in the optimal transport plans for ORC. This results in different local curvature profiles, allowing distinction.
Remark 1: Encoding certain local substructure counts can also distinguish these graphs, but requires careful substructure selection. LCP implicitly characterizes substructure information via local curvature distribution without such fine-tuning. Spectral encodings cannot distinguish them due to identical spectra. LDP encodings cannot due to identical node degree distributions. Random walk-based PE can distinguish them stochastically.
The relationship between ORC distribution and the WL hierarchy is an open question; ORC may distinguish some graphs not distinguishable by higher-order WL tests.

4 Experiments

Experiments demonstrate LCP effectiveness on node and graph classification tasks. Questions:
Q1: Does LCP enhance GNN performance on node- and graph-level tasks?
Q2: Are structural and positional encodings complementary?
Q3: How does LCP compare to curvature-based rewiring in downstream performance?
Ablation studies investigate other curvature notions.

4.1 Experimental Setup
Encoding or rewiring is a preprocessing step. GNNs (GCN, GIN, GAT) are trained on processed graphs. Settings and hyperparameters are held constant across tasks and baselines. Hyperparameter tuning is performed for individual encoding types. For rewiring, heuristics from Fesser et al. (2023) are used. Results are accumulated over 100 random trials. Mean test accuracy and 95% confidence intervals are reported.

4.2 Results

4.2.1 Performance of LCP (Q1)
Table 1 presents graph classification (Enzymes, Imdb, Mutag, Proteins) and node classification (Cora, Citeseer) results with no encodings (NO), Laplacian eigenvectors (LA), Random Walk probabilities (RW), substructures (SUB), and LCP. LCP outperforms all other encodings on all graph classification datasets. Improvements are particularly large for GCN and GAT: mean accuracy increases by 10 to almost 20 percent compared to no encodings, and 4 to 14 percent compared to the second-best encoding. On node classification datasets, LCP is competitive but performance gains are smaller, and other encodings occasionally outperform LCP.

4.2.2 Combining Structural and Positional Encodings (Q2)
Table 2 shows results combining structural encodings (SUB, LCP) with positional encodings (LA, RW). The best-performing combination always includes LCP. Performance gains depend on the model: GCN shows improvement on three of six datasets (largest gain: +7% on Mutag). GIN shows improvement on five of six datasets (largest gain: +3% on Proteins). GAT shows improvement on four of six datasets (gains ≤2%). Combinations generally result in better performance than single encodings. The best positional encoding choice depends on the dataset: RW leads to higher accuracy in 14 of 18 cases, LA in 4 cases.

4.2.3 Comparing Structural Encoding and Rewiring (Q3)
Table 3 shows performance on graphs rewired using BORF (an ORC-based rewiring strategy) with no encodings (NO), LA, or RW. Comparing NO rows in Table 3 with LCP rows in Table 1, using ORC for LCP results in significantly higher accuracy on all datasets than using it for rewiring. Comparing LA and RW rows in Table 3 with (LCP, LA) and (LCP, RW) rows in Table 2, the LCP-based variant outperforms the rewiring-based one on all graph classification datasets. Combining rewiring and positional encodings attains best performance in only two cases on node classification datasets.

LCP and GNN Depth: Figure 1 shows that the average accuracy of a GCN with LCP does not decrease faster with the number of layers than the average accuracy of a GCN on a rewired graph. Both lose between 4 and 5 percent accuracy when moving from 5 to 10 GCN layers.

4.3 Different Notions of Curvature
Table 4 shows graph classification accuracies for GCN with LCP using Forman-Ricci curvature (FRC), Augmented Forman-Ricci curvature considering 3-cycles (AFRC-3), considering 3- and 4-cycles (AFRC-4), and ORC. All four curvatures improve upon the baseline. Performance generally increases from FRC to its augmentations to ORC. FRC is surprisingly effective as a faster substitute for ORC. The choice of which higher-order structures to encode (AFRC-3 vs. AFRC-4) impacts LCP's ability to characterize substructures with higher-order cycles.

5 Discussion and Limitations

This paper introduced Local Curvature Profiles (LCP) as a structural encoding that endows nodes with a geometric characterization of their neighborhoods via discrete curvature. Experiments demonstrated that LCP outperforms existing encoding approaches, and further performance increases are achieved by combining LCP with global positional encodings. Compared to curvature-based rewiring, LCP achieves superior performance.

While LCP improves MPGNN expressivity, the relationship between LCP and the k-WL hierarchy remains open. Experiments revealed differences in encoding effectiveness between GNN architectures. Future work should analyze the influence of model design relative to the graph learning task and input graph topology. Further research on the suitability of different curvature notions for various tasks and graph topologies is needed.

LCP implicitly characterizes substructure information via local curvature distribution without such fine-tuning. Spectral encodings cannot distinguish them due to identical spectra. LDP encodings cannot due to identical node degree distributions. Random walk-based PE can distinguish them stochastically.

Q2: Are structural and positional encodings complementary?
Q3: How does LCP compare to curvature-based rewiring in downstream performance?
Ablation studies investigate other curvature notions.

Encoding or rewiring is a preprocessing step. GNNs (GCN, GIN, GAT) are trained on processed graphs. Settings and hyperparameters are held constant across tasks and baselines. Mean test accuracy and 95% confidence intervals are reported.

On node classification datasets, LCP is competitive but performance gains are smaller, and other encodings occasionally outperform LCP.

The best positional encoding choice depends on the dataset: RW leads to higher accuracy in 14 of 18 cases, LA in 4 cases.

4.2.3 Comparing Structural Encoding and Rewiring (Q3)

LCP and GNN Depth: Figure 1 shows that the average accuracy of a GCN with LCP does not decrease faster with the number of layers than the average accuracy of a GCN on a rewired graph. Both lose between 4 and 5 percent accuracy when moving from 5 to 10 GCN layers.

Table 4 shows graph classification accuracies for GCN with LCP using Forman-Ricci curvature (FRC), Augmented Forman-Ricci curvature considering 3-cycles (AFRC-3), considering 3- and 4-cycles (AFRC-4), and ORC. The choice of which higher-order structures to encode (AFRC-3 vs. AFRC-4) impacts LCP's ability to characterize substructures with higher-order cycles.

5 Discussion and Limitations

This paper introduced Local Curvature Profiles (LCP) as a structural encoding that endows nodes with a geometric characterization of their neighborhoods via discrete curvature. Experiments demonstrated that LCP outperforms existing encoding approaches, and further performance increases are achieved by combining LCP with global positional encodings. Compared to curvature-based rewiring, LCP achieves superior performance.

While LCP improves MPGNN expressivity, the relationship between LCP and the k-WL hierarchy remains open. Experiments revealed differences in encoding effectiveness between GNN architectures. Future work should analyze the influence of model design relative to the graph learning task and input graph topology. Further research on the suitability of different curvature notions for various tasks and graph topologies is needed.
