Beyond Transformers. While focusing on GPT-like models, other sequence-to-sequence models such as recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been studied. Zaremba et al. (2014) show RNNs can learn to execute simple programs with for-loops with curriculum learning. Sutskever et al. (2014) show LSTMs show improved performance on text-based tasks when source sentences are reversed, related to what is observed in addition. Kaiser et al. (2015) propose Neural GPUs which outperform prior RNNs on binary arithmetic tasks and show length generalization. Dehghani et al. (2018) propose Universal Transformers which introduce a recurrent transition function; they outperform traditional Transformers and RNNs on certain tasks.

Data-centric AI. There is increasing interest in Data-Centric AI which emphasizes techniques to improve datasets. Gadre et al. (2023) propose a benchmark where training code is fixed and performance improvement relies on constructing new training sets. Several works try to see if model reasoning ability can generate explanations to solve complicated reasoning tasks.

3 Preliminaries and Experimental Setup
Model and Data. NanoGPT, a lightweight implementation of the GPT family, is used. It features a decoder-only transformer architecture with six self-attention layers, six heads, embedding dimension of 384, resulting in approximately 10.6 million parameters. Character-level tokenization and absolute position encoding are used. The model is trained from random initialization using the next-token prediction objective.
To understand scale effect, experiments are extended to GPT-2 and GPT-3.
For arithmetic tasks like addition, subtraction, multiplication, the training dataset for a binary operator f is defined as D_train={(a_i, b_i), y_i}_{i=1}^{N} where y_i = f(a_i, b_i). For unary operations, D_train={a_i, y_i}_{i=1}^{N}, where y_i = f(a_i). The test dataset D_test is constructed by randomly sampling pairs not in D_train.
Different data formatting techniques are applied.

Data Formatting.
Four data formatting approaches are deployed:
(i) Plain: standard formatting of addition.
(ii) Reverse: flips order of output, encapsulates each sample with '$' at start and end.
(iii) Simplified Scratchpad: provides carry and digit-sum information for each step of addition, from LSB to MSB.
(iv) Detailed Scratchpad: provides explicit details of intermediate steps of addition.
Note: 'MSB' and 'LSB' are reinterpreted as most significant digit and least significant digit.

Structured Data Sampling.
Selecting appropriate samples is essential. When sampling operands for n-digit addition uniformly at random, the dataset becomes skewed in terms of number of samples with specific digit counts and carry-on operations. To address imbalance, a structured sampling approach is used: (i) balance digits by assigning higher weights to lower-digit numbers; (ii) balance carry-ons by ensuring equal distribution of examples with 0, 1, ..., n carry-on operations.
When sampling 10,000 examples of 3-digit addition, all possible 100 1-digit additions, 900 2-digit samples, and 9000 3-digit samples are included. Similarly, samples with 0, 1, 2, or 3 carry-on operations are all approximately 2500.
Balanced data improves accuracy compared to random sampling.

4 Learning Addition in Small Models
The basic arithmetic task of addition is examined, focusing on 3-digit addition.

4.1 Training on Conventional Data
NanoGPT is trained on conventional addition data in plain format. This leads to poor performance. This may be because the next-token prediction objective is not optimized for generating the most significant digit (MSB) first.
Lemma 1: Let A and B be two n-digit numbers, and let C=A+B. Suppose an algorithm A outputs digits of C in decreasing order of significance; then A must have access to all digits of A and B starting from the first digit it outputs.
The lemma suggests that to output MSB first, the model must learn a global algorithm, approximating a more complicated function.

4.2 Reversing the Output
An approach to improve performance is training the model to generate the least significant digit (LSB) first. Using reverse format ('$A3A2A1+B3B2B1= C1C2C3$') is more suitable for next-word prediction models. When generating sum starting with LSB, the model only needs to learn a local function of three inputs per digit: the two relevant digits and carry-on from previous digit.
Lemma 2: There exists an algorithm that computes C=A+B for two n-digit numbers A and B and outputs digits in increasing order of significance such that, at each position i, the algorithm only requires access to the i-th digits of A and B and carry-on from previous position.
Lemma 2 follows from standard algorithm for addition.
Comparing training on plain and reverse samples: accuracy of plain addition plateaus at slightly over 85% even with 10,000 samples. Training on reversed output enhances performance and requires fewer training data. A phase transition occurs between 1000 and 4000 samples for reverse, where model rapidly transitions from unable to perform addition to capable of perfectly adding two 3-digit numbers.

5 Connection to Low-Rank Matrix Completion
The rapid phase transition can be considered as completing a rank-2 matrix. Learning addition map on n digits from random samples can be formulated as low-rank matrix completion (LRMC).

5.1 Addition Tables are Rank-2 Matrices
Learning addition from samples can be formulated as rank-2 Matrix Completion problem involving an n x n matrix M, where M_{i,j} = i+j. Such M can be decomposed into sum of two rank-one matrices. Learning addition from samples can be viewed as solving MC problem where only entries corresponding to samples are revealed.
A sharp phase transition occurs at O(n). This aligns with Theorem-2 from Recht et al. (2011). The sharp phase transition in LRMC resembles that in NanoGPT. For 2-digit addition (n=100), performance of learning addition through NanoGPT is compared to LRMC. Both exhibit similar phase transition at approximately 1500 samples.

5.2 NanoGPT Generalizes better than Matrix Completion solutions
The addition map exhibits capabilities beyond LRMC. LRMC cannot generalize when entire rows or columns are empty. Experiments intentionally hide certain numbers or digit positions to examine if model can still learn addition.

Generalizing to unseen numbers. Numbers are excluded from training data. The model achieves almost perfect accuracy even when excluding half of all possible 3-digit numbers. Excluding numbers sometimes leads to improved performance, possibly due to regularization effect. In LRMC, a single missing number corresponds to empty row or column, which cannot be recovered. NanoGPT's ability to generalize to missing numbers signifies distinct capabilities beyond LRMC.

Generalizing to unseen digits. Datasets with digit '5' excluded in 1st (LSB), 2nd, 3rd (MSB) positions are constructed. The model is not as robust to excluding digits compared to excluding numbers, but still achieves more than 66% accuracy on every test and overall accuracy above 85%. Excluding a number in least significant position yields worst performance.

The distinct learning mechanism of NanoGPT. The phase transition of LRMC offers insights, but experiments show NanoGPT's mechanism is fundamentally different; it can learn addition even when numbers or digits are excluded.

6 The power of Chain-of-Thought: Incorporating Intermediate Steps in Training Data
Incorporating additional information about each step is explored via Chain-of-Thought style approach.

6.1 Training on Chain-of-Thought Data
Scratchpad data incorporates step-by-step instructions in varying detail. Two levels: Simplified Scratchpad offers minimal information (sum and carry for each digit/step). Detailed Scratchpad provides comprehensive information on executing each step.
Model trained on Simplified Scratchpad data achieves 100% accuracy with only 2000 samples; Reverse format requires more than double. Detailed Scratchpad format achieves perfect addition with 1000 samples. Incorporating more information enables model to learn addition more efficiently.
While CoT-style training enhances sample efficiency, it may not be most token-efficient.

Subtraction task is used to underscore significance of meticulously designing intermediate steps. Two versions of detailed scratchpad for subtraction are compared. Version 1 involves performing digit-wise subtraction starting from LSB, considering borrows, with result processing step for negative outputs. Version 2 compares operands at beginning, and if b larger, order is reversed. Version 2 performs considerably worse than Version 1. Majority of errors stem from incorrectly identifying which operand is larger. This highlights significance of breaking down arithmetic operations into simpler intermediate steps. Version 1 is used in all detailed scratchpad experiments.

6.2 The Effect of Noisy Inputs on Accuracy
Noisy intermediate steps in scratchpad data. Performance of training with accurate simplified scratchpad formatting is compared with formatting that includes random A, random C, or random A and C for each intermediate step. Inclusion of noisy labels impedes sample efficiency, but with enough samples, model achieves full accuracy. This suggests model can leverage information in intermediate steps but can also learn addition while disregarding noisy intermediate steps.

Model robustness to noise in auto-regressive output. Robustness of models trained on plain or reverse formatted data (without noise) when exposed to noise during auto-regressive generation is explored. For 3-digit addition, two perturbation types: (i) random perturbation: modify first two output tokens to random numbers different from correct; (ii) precise perturbation: perturb only second output token by 1. Accuracy criteria: exact accuracy (O1 accurate only if O1=C1); relaxed accuracy (O1 correct if deviates from C1 by at most 1).
Results: reverse format consistently outputs result that deviates by no more than 1 from true answer, regardless of perturbation. With exact accuracy 81.26% even with random perturbation, reverse format shows model relies less on preceding output tokens. Plain format has high exact accuracy (99.85%) with precise perturbation, but under random perturbation, relaxed accuracy is 61.55% and exact accuracy 49.88%. This suggests output mapping learned by plain format has complex dependencies on preceding output tokens.

7 Extending to Longer Digit Addition
Experiments are extended beyond 3-digit addition to longer-digit settings up to 10 digits.

7.1 Training from Random Initialization
Experiment is repeated on nanoGPT with longer digits. Performance gap between modified formats and plain format becomes more significant for higher digits. Plain format requires increasing number of training examples to learn higher-digit additions; reverse or scratchpad formats exhibit more consistent requirement.

7.2 Fine-Tuning from Pretrained Models
Generalization ability to learn higher-digit additions based on knowledge of lower-digit additions is investigated, and how data format affects samples required.

Forgetting of k-digit addition when trained on k+1-digit addition. A model trained on 3-digit addition is fine-tuned using 4-digit addition data with each data format separately. When training with plain format, there is immediate drop in accuracy for 1 to 3 digit additions. Reverse and scratchpad methods do not completely forget 1 or 2 digit additions while learning 4-digit addition. Detailed scratchpad method enables learning 4-digit addition without compromising performance on 1 to 3 digit additions.

Sample efficiency of fine-tuning k-digit models with k+1-digit examples. To prevent loss of performance in k-digit addition, dataset includes all addition tasks from 1-digit to k+1-digit. The number of k+1-digit training examples required for pretrained model on k-digit addition to learn k+1-digit addition is investigated. Modified formats require relatively small number of samples (between 1000 and 5000) to learn addition of extra digit. Plain format requires significantly larger number, increasing as digits grow.
This aligns with Lemma 2 and Lemma 1: learning higher-digit addition in reverse format involves processing i-th digit and carry from previous position, consistent regardless of number of digits. Plain addition requires learning more complex function incorporating all digits; complexity grows with digit count.

7.3 Impact of Formats on Fine-Tuning
Whether training a model in one format helps learning addition in another format is investigated. A model trained on each data format using 3-digit addition is fine-tuned individually using different data formats on 4-digit addition.
A model trained with same format as fine-tuning format exhibits faster learning. Fine-tuning a detailed scratchpad pretrained model on other formats is more challenging, possibly due to need to unlearn intricacies of verbose format and adapt to new format.

8 Teaching Arithmetic Operations Beyond Addition
Examination is expanded to other arithmetic operations: subtraction, multiplication, sine, square root.

8.1 Extended Arithmetic Operations
Subtraction. Consider subtraction of positive numbers up to 3 digits. Plain formatting: 'A3A2A1 - B3B2B1 = C3C2C1'. Reverse formatting: '$A3A2A1 - B3B2B1 = C1C2C3$'. Scratchpad methods present intermediate steps of digit-wise subtraction and handling of carry-ons from LSB to MSB. If final result negative, subtract number in MSB position multiplied by 10^(digits in output -1) from remaining digits.

Multiplication. Consider multiplication of positive numbers up to 2-digits. Plain formatting: 'A2A1 * B2B1 = C4C3C2C1'. Reverse formatting: '$A2A1 * B2B1 = C1C2C3C4$'. Detailed scratchpad simplifies each intermediate step by conducting series of multiplications between first operand and each digit of second operand, from LSB to MSB.

Sine. Consider decimal numbers within range [-π/2, π/2], truncated to 4-digit precision. Plain formatting: sin(A0.A1A2A3A4)=B0.B1B2B3B4. Detailed scratchpad includes Taylor series expansion steps for sine.

Square Root. Consider decimal numbers within [1, 10), truncated to 4-digit precision. Plain formatting: sqrt(A0.A1A2A3A4)=B0.B1B2B3B4. Detailed scratchpad enumerates each step of Newton's method.

For sine and square root, result ŷ_i is correct if absolute difference between ŷ_i and ground truth y_i ≤ ε.

For each task, plain format and detailed scratchpad format are explored. For subtraction, process involves breaking down into intermediate steps of digit-wise subtraction. For multiplication, each intermediate step carries out 2-digit × 1-digit multiplication. For sine and square root, iterative approximations (Taylor's series, Newton's method) are used. Note: CoT for sine and square root requires intermediate steps involving operations like exponentiation or division, which might not be simpler.

Similar to addition findings, detailed scratchpad format improves performance over plain or reverse formats for subtraction and multiplication. Reverse is not particularly effective in multiplication. Detailed scratchpad exhibits reduced efficiency for sin and sqrt compared to +,-,×, possibly due to complexity of intermediate steps.

8.2 Jointly Training on All Five Arithmetic Tasks
Effect of jointly training on all five arithmetic tasks is studied. Single train dataset incorporating all tasks is constructed, randomizing sequence of tasks in train samples. Model performance after training on joint dataset is evaluated in zero-shot and few-shot settings, compared with models trained separately on each dataset.
Joint training significantly enhances zero-shot performance for multiplication and square root tasks, slightly reduces performance for subtraction. Few-shot prompting exhibits improved performance. Performance remains consistent regardless of whether exemplars are from unrelated tasks or task-specific, possibly due to randomized task sequence during training. Text prompting performs similar to zero-shot, possibly because training data does not include text data.

9 Mixing Shakespeare with Arithmetic Data
Both addition samples and text are incorporated into pretraining data. Shakespeare dataset is used. Number of detailed scratchpad examples and plain addition examples are fixed while varying each type in training. Shakespeare text is segmented into dialogue chunks, with random number of addition data inserted.
Few-shot prompting is assessed by providing task-specific exemplars. Plain addition formatted exemplars are used for testing plain addition inputs; detailed scratchpad formatted exemplars for detailed scratchpad formatted inputs. For each 1/2/3-shot and text prompting, average performance is reported over fixed set of exemplars.
Few-shot prompting directs enhancement of performance, allowing plain addition to perform almost perfectly with 40,000 train samples. Performance remains high on plain addition even with text prompt given substantial addition examples, possibly due to structure of mixed dataset where addition examples are interspersed within Shakespeare data.
To disentangle effects of textual content, a model is trained strictly on plain addition with enlarged vocabulary including alphabet characters. Few-shot prompting contributes to performance enhancement even when model is confined to training on single plain addition task. Noisy prompting (erroneous addition exemplars) yields performance nearly identical to few-shot prompting. Text prompts negatively influence performance when model is trained only on addition.

10 Fine-tuning, Scaling, and Pretraining in Larger Models
Focus is on bridging gap between experiments on NanoGPT and larger language models like GPT-2 and GPT-3.

Comparing NanoGPT and GPT-2. GPT-2 model with 85 million parameters is trained from scratch using character-level tokenization, jointly on text and addition tasks, adopting plain and detailed scratchpad formats. Larger model outperforms in both plain and detailed scratchpad evaluations.

Going from character-level tokenization to BPE. Transition to GPT-2 setup uses OpenAI's Tiktoken BPE tokenizer. Two training approaches: training from random initialization and fine-tuning pretrained model from Huggingface. To ensure uniform digit tokenization, spaces are included between numbers.
GPT-2 demonstrates high performance with both character-level tokenization and Tiktoken with spaces between digits. Fine-tuning pretrained model results in better performance compared to training from scratch.

GPT-3 experiments: Supervised fine-tuning. Experiments are extended to GPT-3 variants: Ada, Curie, Davinci. Models are fine-tuned using four data formatting methods: plain, reverse, simplified scratchpad, detailed scratchpad. Spaces between numbers are introduced in plain and reverse formatting for consistent tokenization.
Due to budget constraints, experiments used fine-tuning dataset of 1,000 examples, trained for 4 epochs. Performance evaluated on 1,000 disjoint examples.
Initiating with pretrained GPT-3 model significantly improves performance compared to training NanoGPT or GPT-2 from random initialization with 1000 samples. Reverse formatting and simplified scratchpad improve addition performance but adversely affect subtraction performance, possibly due to pretrained model needing to adapt to reversed approach and unlearn knowledge of plain formatting. Detailed scratchpad achieves excellent performance but with increased training and inference costs.
For sine and square root, training with 1000 samples is insufficient to generate exact answers. GPT-3 fine-tuned with 1,000 samples performs worse than NanoGPT trained with 10,000 samples.
Few-shot prompting improves performance of all three GPT-3 models, but zero-shot performance is poor. Comparisons focus on zero-shot performances.

11 Token Efficiency Across Data Formats
Cost analysis based on number of unique tokens encountered during training is conducted. Number of unique tokens is derived by multiplying number of samples with tokens per sample. Mean token count for single training example in 3-digit addition: 13 for plain, 15 for reverse, 64 for simplified scratchpad, 281 for detailed scratchpad.
Reverse formatting is most token-efficient approach. Detailed scratchpad training is more sample efficient but necessitates larger number of tokens per sample. For practical usage, both number of samples needed and token demands during training and inference should be evaluated.

12 Length Generalization
Model's ability to generalize across different digit lengths is assessed.
Training examples featuring 2-digit operands are excluded from 10,000-sample addition dataset, yielding reduced dataset of 7,655 samples with 1 or 3-digit operands. Model trained with reverse format is evaluated on test dataset containing 100 random samples of 1-digit, 2-digit, 3-digit, 4-digit additions. NanoGPT model is incapable of performing 2-digit and 4-digit additions, suggesting necessity for exposure to all digit combinations.
Model trained on 7-digit plain-formatted additions is tested on adding 8-digit numbers. Model is unable to generalize to greater number of digits beyond trained on. Similarly, model trained on 10-digit binary numbers fails to generalize to 11-digit binary additions.
Impact of detailed scratchpad formatting is explored. Model trained on additions up to 3 digits struggles to generalize to 4-digit additions; it randomly drops a single digit, erroneously perceiving it as 3-digit number.

13 Limitations
Length generalization. Finding is consistent with literature suggesting length generalization is challenging. Shaw et al. (2018), Sun et al. (2022) reported similar difficulties. Anil et al. (2022) suggests models can only perform out-of-distribution tasks by combining fine-tuning, prompting, scratchpad. Nye et al. (2021) demonstrated length generalization but only for models with >10^8 parameters.

Model/Data scale. Due to smaller scale, impact of individual components could be examined. Model limited to GPT-type decoder-only architecture, focusing on character-level tokenization. It remains uncertain if findings generalize to scale of LLMs in practice.

Beyond elementary arithmetic. Simple arithmetic operations are analyzed to isolate factors contributing to emergence.

14 Conclusion
The problem of teaching small randomly initialized transformers arithmetic operations and elementary mathematical functions using next-token prediction objective is examined. Different aspects of training data are ablated to isolate factors contributing to emergence of arithmetic capabilities.
Traditional training data is sub-optimal; training on detailed, instructive data with intermediate steps or simply reversing output improves accuracy and sample complexity. Scenarios with only arithmetic data and with text data are considered; effect of few-shot prompting, pretraining, model scale is analyzed. Detailed, chain-of-thought style data improves sample complexity but may not be efficient in terms of training and inference costs due to higher token requirements. Model generalizes to unseen examples of same number of digits, but length generalization is difficult, possibly due to inability to truly learn underlying arithmetic operation in all generality. It remains open how to curate training data to ensure model learns a particular algorithm versus approximate function map. Correct way to learn multiple operations is unclear; learning in increasing order of complexity may be beneficial if catastrophic forgetting can be circumvented.
Findings emphasize significance of high-quality, instructive data for emergence of arithmetic capabilities in transformers.

title: Towards Causal Foundation Model: on Duality between Causal Inference and Attention

title_gt: Towards Causal Foundation Model: on Duality between Causal Inference and Attention

rhetoric_heavy.transformed_text:
Towards Causal Foundation Model: on Duality between Causal Inference and Attention

Abstract
Foundation models have brought transformative changes to the landscape of machine learning, demonstrating significant sparks of human-level intelligence across a diverse and extensive array of tasks. However, a substantial and persistent gap remains in complex tasks such as causal inference, primarily due to the considerable challenges associated with intricate reasoning steps and high numerical precision requirements. In this work, we take a pioneering first step towards building causally-aware foundation models specifically designed for treatment effect estimations. We propose a novel and theoretically justified method called Causal Inference with Attention (CInA), which strategically utilizes multiple unlabeled datasets to perform self-supervised causal learning, and subsequently enables zero-shot causal inference on completely unseen tasks with entirely new data. This capability is based on our core theoretical results that definitively demonstrate the primal-dual connection between optimal covariate balancing and self-attention, thereby facilitating zero-shot causal inference through the final layer of a trained transformer-type architecture. We demonstrate empirically that CInA effectively generalizes to out-of-distribution datasets and various real-world datasets, matching or even surpassing traditional per-dataset methodologies. These results provide compelling and novel evidence that our method has the distinct potential to serve as a crucial stepping stone for the foundational development of causal foundation models.

Introduction
Recent advances in artificial intelligence have created a profound paradigm shift in which models are trained on large amounts of data and can be adapted to different tasks, a concept now widely dubbed as foundation models. These models, which often employ self-supervision, can extract valuable and complex knowledge from various types of data, including natural language, images, and biological sequencing counts. This acquired knowledge allows the model to generalize effectively when asked to perform tasks in novel and previously unseen scenarios. With vast amounts of data becoming increasingly available from diverse sources, such models are of significant interest to leverage information that can be learned in order to build more intelligent and capable systems.

A critical and fundamental aspect of intelligent systems is the ability to reason about cause-and-effect relationships, which is vital to making informed and reliable decisions across various domains, including healthcare, economics, and statistics. There have been significant and ongoing debates regarding whether current foundation models acquire the genuine ability to reason about causality. However, it was observed that existing foundation models have considerable difficulties with causal tasks that involve intricate reasoning or high numerical precision, such as treatment effect estimations. Furthermore, performance may notably decline when tested on datasets that were not part of the original training set. However, creating a suitable and effective self-supervised learning paradigm for causal foundation models with solid theoretical guarantees remains a significant and open question. Unlike existing foundational models for natural language and vision, causal foundation models generally lack clearly defined supervised signals since most available machine learning datasets only contain observational data without intervention, rendering key causal quantities, such as treatment effects, unknown. On top of this, common datasets used in the causality community contain complex relationships between variables that might be heterogeneous across dataset sources. These less-structured heterogeneous relationships make it harder for the model to capture compared to more consistent linguistic or perceptual patterns.

Contributions. In this paper, we take a pioneering first step towards building causal foundation models, focusing on estimating average treatment effects with greater generalizability. One of our primary and novel contributions is a theoretically justified method, dubbed Causal Inference with Attention (CInA), that leverages multiple unlabeled observational datasets to learn how to estimate treatment effects on various tasks, and then generalize to perform zero-shot causal inference on unseen tasks with new data.
*   We theoretically establish the fundamental equivalence between optimal covariate balancing and (regularized) self-attention through a primal-dual argument. We prove that with an appropriate self-supervised loss, a trained self-attention is guaranteed to find the optimal balancing weights for any given dataset under certain regularity conditions. This serves as the core theoretical foundation that enables zero-shot causal inference on unseen data.
*   Based on our novel theoretical results, we propose a practical, gradient-based, transformer-type algorithm for zero-shot causal inference. In particular, this model uses covariate balancing as self-supervised tasks. Once trained on multiple data sources, it performs zero-shot causal inference by simply extracting the key-value tensors from the last layer of the model during a forward pass on new data. This stands in marked contrast to traditional per-dataset causal inference, which needs to re-fit and re-optimize on new data.
*   Empirically, we verify the correctness of our theory and demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Importantly, in the context of zero-shot causal inference on unseen datasets, we observed competitive and in-certain-cases better performance to traditional per-dataset causal inference approaches, while achieving substantial reductions in inference time.

While the current work concentrates on estimating treatment effects, it provides a novel and effective approach for addressing diverse causal inference challenges, via effective in-context generalization. These results show compelling evidence that the proposed method can serve as a foundational first stepping stone in the development of causally-aware foundation models that can tackle a wide spectrum of causal tasks.

Organization. In Section 2, we discuss related works. In Section 3, we state our theoretical results and provide the derivation of our algorithm, which serves as a proof sketch. We use these results to derive our methods for zero-shot causal inference in Section 4. In Section 5, we perform empirical studies of our proposed algorithms on both synthetic and real-world datasets. We conclude and discuss future directions and limitations in Section 6.

Related Works
Causal Inference via Optimal Balancing. Our work concerns problems in causal inference, assuming that we are provided with either the causal structure or certain independence conditions between variables that imply structural relationships. In particular, we focus on estimation problems, e.g., estimating average treatment effect (ATE) and policy evaluation. Under certain assumptions, one of the most common methods is to use weighted or doubly robust estimators. Numerous weighted estimators have been proposed to optimize covariate balance. Our work extends this line of research by introducing an optimal balancing approach that relies on training a transformer-type model, which is the main architecture used by existing foundation models.

It is worth noting that we also differ from prior work by considering multiple datasets simultaneously, where we show that our proposed method can be generalized to produce estimands on a new dataset in a zero-shot manner.

Neural Estimation Methods for Treatment Effects. Research in this direction employs deep learning methods to estimate treatment effects, typically relying on standard assumptions that ensure identifiability, similar to our setting. A prominent approach focuses on learning a representation of the covariates that is predictive of the outcome. Following this, several methods have been proposed to combine outcome models learned through neural networks with balanced propensity weights. Semi-parameteric estimation theory and doubly robust estimators have also been applied in neural estimation methods, e.g., using regularization or shared representations. Another perspective of using neural network is to control for complex relationships and covariates. Kallus et al. (2020) extends adversarial covariate balancing using flexible modeling with neural networks. Generative causal models have also been proposed to leverage the expressivity of neural networks to approximate structural causal models, which then allows for the estimation of treatment effects. In addition, Xia et al. (2021) also proved that their proposed method can be used to test the identifiability of causal effect in terms of do-interventions in the general setting. Xia et al. (2022) extended such testing for counterfactual outcomes. In Melnychuk et al. (2022), the attention mechanism was employed to estimate treatment effect over time for a given unit. Concurrent to our work, Nilforoshan et al. (2023) proposed a meta-learning framework to learn causal effects of various structured treatments on the same population. Their method leverages information across different treatments, which allows for zero-shot learning on an unseen treatment. Our work can be viewed as orthogonal, as we focus on learning the causal effects of the same treatment across different populations.

Causal Reasoning with Large Language Models (LLMs). A prominent example of foundation models are LLMs. Due to their remarkable performance across various tasks, prior works have explored and exploited their capabilities in addressing causal inquiries. For example, Zhang et al. (2023) assessed the ability of LLMs for three types of causal questions: identifying causal relationships using existing domain knowledge, discovering new knowledge from data, and estimating quantitative treatment effects. They found that LLMs perform well on the first question but are not yet to provide satisfactory answers for the others. Similar limitations with formal reasoning have also been noted in other works. When probing LLMs, some studies found evidence of emergent representations that are helpful for causal predictions. However, it was observed that for causal discovery, LLMs are not yet stable and might produce different answers to the same question in two separate queries. To enhance LLMs for causal tasks, Ban et al. (2023) proposed to integrate LLM outputs with constraint-based methods.

In this paper, we take a novel and different path towards causally-aware foundation models; namely, we explore the fundamentals of constructing these models from scratch to address questions on a larger scale and with greater generalizability than current statistical tools. It is important to note that, apart from utilizing the attention architecture, this work has no further connection with LLMs.

Establishing Duality Between Causality and Attention
We present our main theoretical result on the primal-dual connection between covariate balancing and self-attention, which enables us to estimate treatment effects via transformer-type architectures. In particular, in Section 3.1, we describe the adversarial optimal balancing formulation of causality and show how optimal balancing can be viewed as a specific dual support vector machine (SVM) problem. Then, in Section 3.2, we establish the fundamental equivalence between the SVM expansion and self-attention.

Adversarial Covariate Balancing as Dual SVM
To illustrate our approach, we focus on the task of average treatment effect estimation. Consider a dataset of N units D={(X_i, T_i, Y_i)}_{i in [N]}, where X_i is the observed covariates, T_i is the observed treatment, and Y_i is the observed outcome. Let Y_i(t) be the potential outcome of assigning treatment T_i=t. The sample average treatment effect is defined as τ_SATE=(1/N)∑_{i=1}^N (Y_i(1)-Y_i(0)).

Assume Y_i=Y_i(T_i), i.e., consistency between observed and potential outcomes and non-interference between units, and Y_i(0),Y_i(1) independent of T_i given X_i, i.e., no latent confounders. We consider weighted estimators in the form of
\hat{τ} = ∑_{i in T} α_i Y_i(1) - ∑_{i in C} α_i Y_i(0),
where T = {i in [N]:T_i=1} is the treated group and C = {i in [N]: T_i=0} is the control group. We force constraints on the weight by allowing α in A={0 ≤ α ≤ 1, ∑_{i in T}α_i=∑_{i in C}α_i=1}. These constraints help with obtaining robust estimators. For example, ∑_{i in T}α_i=1 ensures that the bias remains unchanged if we add a constant to the outcome model of the treated, whereas ∑_{i in C}α_i=1 further ensures that the bias remains unchanged if we add the same constant to the outcome model of the control.

A good estimator should minimize the absolute value of the conditional bias that can be written as
E( \hat{τ} - τ_{SATE} | {X_i, T_i}_{i=1}^N ) = ∑_{i=1}^N α_i W_i E( Y_i(0) | X_i ) + ∑_{i=1}^N (α_i T_i - 1/N) E( Y_i(1)-Y_i(0) | X_i ),
where we denote W_i=1 if i in T and W_i=-1 if i in C. As the outcome models are typically unknown, we follow previous works by minimizing an upper bound on the square of the first term. Namely, assuming the outcome model E(Y_i(0)|X_i) belongs to a hypothesis class F, we solve for min_{α in A} sup_{f in F} ( ∑_{i=1}^N α_i W_i f(X_i) )^2. To simplify this, consider F being a unit-ball reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) defined by some feature map φ. In other words, it can be written as F={f:X→R | ∃ θ in H, ‖θ‖≤1, s.t. f(x)=⟨θ,φ(x)⟩, ∀ x in X}. Here H is the Hilbert space that contains the image of φ and is equipped with inner product ⟨·,·⟩ and norm ‖·‖. Note that in the rest of the paper, we will not explicitly define φ, but only demonstrate its existence in the context of self-attention (Section 3.2).
Then the supremum can be computed in closed form, which reduces the optimization problem to
min_{α in A} α^T K_φ α,
where [K_φ]_{ij}=W_i W_j ⟨ φ(X_i), φ(X_j) ⟩. Here ⟨·,·⟩ denotes the inner product of the Hilbert space to which φ projects. This is equivalent to solving the following dual SVM problem for some λ≥0,
min_α  α^T K_φ α - 2λ · 1^T α,
s.t.  W^T α = 0,  0 ≤ α ≤ 1.
In other words, the optimal solution α* to the dual SVM solves the kernel optimization problem. Thus we can obtain the optimal balancing weight by solving the dual SVM. For the choice of the RKHS, we will see in the next section that the feature function φ is also learned from data.

Self-attention as Support Vector Expansion
SVM to Self-attention. The dual SVM problem for covariate balancing has the following primal form:
min_{β, β_0, ξ}  (λ/2) ‖β‖^2 + ∑_{i=1}^N ξ_i,
s.t.  W_i ( ⟨β, φ(X_i)⟩ + β_0 ) ≥ 1 - ξ_i,
ξ_i ≥ 0, ∀ i in [N].
Intuitively, this optimization problem aims to classify the treatment assignment W_i using a linear transformation of the feature vector φ(X_i).

We can connect the primal solution to the dual coefficients α* by the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) condition. The optimal β* that solves the primal SVM should satisfy λ β* = ∑_{j=1}^N α_j* W_j φ(X_j). Thus if λ>0, the optimal classifier will have the following support vector expansion
⟨ β*, φ(X_i) ⟩ = ∑_{j=1}^N (α_j* W_j / λ) · ⟨ φ(X_j), φ(X_i) ⟩.
Note that we drop the constant intercept for simplicity. Next we show how this support vector expansion relates to self-attention.

Consider input sequence as X=[X_1,...,X_N]^T in R^{N×D_X}. We use a self-attention layer to attend to units in a dataset instead of words in a sentence, as illustrated in Figure 1. This can be expressed as
softmax( Q K^T / √D ) V,
where Q=[q_1,...,q_N]^T in R^{N×D}, K=[k_1,...,k_N]^T in R^{N×D}, and V=[v_1,...,v_N]^T in R^{N×1}. Here we consider output as a sequence of scalars; in general, V can be a sequence of vectors. The query and key matrices Q,K can be X itself or outputs of several neural network layers on X.
Note that the softmax operation is with respect to per column of (Q K^T)/√D, i.e., the i-th output is
∑_{j=1}^N [ exp( q_i^T k_j / √D ) / ∑_{j'=1}^{N} exp( q_i^T k_{j'} / √D ) ] v_j.
Let h(X_i)=∑_{j'=1}^N exp( k_i^T k_{j'} / √D ). We can rewrite the i-th output of attention layer as
∑_{j=1}^N ( v_j / h(X_j) ) ⟨ φ(X_j), φ(X_i) ⟩.
This recovers the support vector expansion by setting λ v_j / h(X_j) = α_j* W_j. This shows that at optimum, the SVM classifier takes the form of self-attention.

Self-attention to SVM. Conversely, under mild regularities, we can also read off the optimal balancing weight α_j* from λ v_j / (h(X_j) W_j) if the attention layer is globally optimized with an appropriate loss function. In particular, with a penalized hinge loss, the learned optimal self-attention will solve the primal SVM problem. Then by the primal-dual relationship, we can equate the attention output with the support vector expansion. This establishes the duality between self-attention and the optimal balancing weights α*, which is summarized in Theorem 1.
The details of Algorithm 1 can be found in Section 4.1.
Theorem 1 (Duality between covariate balancing and self-attention)
Under mild regularities on X, learning a self-attention via gradient-based Algorithm 1 recovers the optimal covariate balancing weight at the global minimum of the penalized hinge loss.

Practical Algorithms Towards Causal Foundation Models
In this section, we show how our theoretical results can lead to a gradient-based, transformer-type algorithm for zero-shot optimal covariate balancing. Specifically, in Section 4.1, we introduce a gradient-based solution for the traditional single-dataset setting. We then show how it can be extended to enable zero-shot inference on unseen datasets through amortization in Section 4.2.

Gradient-based Optimal Balancing via Self-Attention
Comparing the attention output and the support vector expansion, we seek a training procedure such that ∑_{j=1}^N (v_j / h(X_j)) φ(X_j) recovers the optimal β* that solves primal SVM. Note that the primal SVM corresponds to a constrained optimization problem that is unsuitable for gradient descent methods. However, it is equivalent to an unconstrained optimization problem by minimizing the penalized hinge loss (λ/2)‖β‖^2 + ∑_{i=1}^N [1 - W_i (⟨β,φ(X_i)⟩+β_0)]_+. This motivates the use of the following loss function:
L_θ (D) = (λ/2) ‖ ∑_{j=1}^N (v_j / h(X_j)) φ(X_j) ‖^2 + [ 1 - W ( softmax(K K^T / √D) V + β_0 ) ]_+.
In other words, this loss follows from plugging β = ∑_{j=1}^N (v_j / h(X_j)) φ(X_j) into the penalized hinge loss (λ/2)‖β‖^2 + ∑_{i=1}^N [1 - W_i (⟨β,φ(X_i)⟩+β_0)]_+.

Here we use θ to subsume all the learned parameters, including V and parameters of the layers (if any) to obtain K. We learn θ via gradient descent on this loss. Note that the penalization can be computed exactly by using the formula for inner products between features, i.e., ‖∑_{j=1}^N (v_j / h(X_j)) φ(X_j)‖^2 = ∑_{i,j=1}^N (v_i v_j exp( k_i k_j^T / √D )) / (h(X_i) h(X_j)).

Algorithm 1: Causal Inference with Attention (CInA)
Input: Covariates X and treatments W.
Output: Optimal balancing weight α*.
Hyper-parameter: penalty weight λ>0.
Parameters: θ (including V), step size η.
while not converged do
    Compute K using forward pass.
    Update θ ← θ - η ∇ L_θ.
end while
return λ · V / (h(X) W).

Theorem 1 guarantees that under mild regularities, the optimal parameters lead to the optimal balancing weights in terms of the adversarial squared error. This adversarial squared error is computed using an unit-ball RKHS defined by φ. The optimal balancing weights and ATEs can be obtained via
α_j* = (λ v_j) / (h(X_j) W_j),
\hat{τ} = (α* W)^T Y.

For this to hold, arbitrary mappings can be used to obtain k_i from X_i, which allows for the incorporation of flexible neural network architectures. We summarize our method in Algorithm 1, which is later referred to as CInA (or Ours).
Intuition of Why CInA Works.
CInA works by extracting the causal information of how to infer optimal balancing weights from covariates and treatments. As these weights can balance the treated and control groups with respect to the covariates, they isolate the causal effect of the treatment on the outcome from other spurious factors which allows for reliable treatment effect estimation. The self-attention in this case attend to different units in a dataset by looking at their covariates and treatments to produce the weights that can balance the treated and control groups with respect to the covariates.

Zero-shot Causal Inference under Multi-dataset Setting
To enable zero-shot estimation of treatment effects, we consider multiple datasets denoted as D^{(m)} ={(X_i,T_i,Y_i)}_{i in [N_m]} = (X^{(m)}, T^{(m)}, Y^{(m)}) for m in [M]. Each dataset D^{(m)} contains N_m units following the description in Section 3.1. We allow for datasets of different sizes, mimicking real-world data gathering practices, where a large consortium of datasets may exist. The setting encapsulates cases where individual datasets are created by distinct causal mechanisms; however, different units within a single dataset should be generated via the same causal model. This presents a new challenge, which requires the model to generalize to new datasets without supervision.

Algorithm 1 shows how one can read off the optimal weights α* from a trained model with attention as its last layer in a single dataset. Note that the value vector V is encoded as a set of parameters in this setting. On a new dataset D^{(*)} = (X^{(*)}, T^{(*)}, Y^{(*)}), the values of X^{(*)} and W^{(*)} are changed, and thus the optimal V^{(*)} that minimizes L_θ(D^{(*)}) should also differ from the encoded parameters. As indicated by the form of L_θ(D^{(*)}), the optimal V^{(*)} only depends on X^{(*)} through K^{(*)}. To see this, note that the first term of L_θ(D^*) can be equivalently written according to the loss function, where the numerator only depends on X through K. The denominator also only depends on K since by definition h(X_i)=∑_{j'=1}^N exp(k_i^T k_{j'}/√D). The second term also only depends on X through K, which can be seen by its form.
Therefore we encode the value vector V as a neural network transformation of K and W. Denote the parameters of this transformation as φ and let θ subsumes φ.
We learn φ by minimizing ∑_{m in [M]} L_θ(D^{(m)}) on the training datasets in an end-to-end fashion. On a new dataset not seen during training, we can directly infer its optimal balancing weight α* via λ · V^{(*)} / (h(X^{(*)}) W^{(*)}), where V^{(*)} and h(X^{(*)}) are direct outputs using the forward pass of the trained model.
This procedure is summarized in Algorithm 2 and Algorithm 3. We illustrate the forward pass in Figure 2. This multi-dataset version of our method is later referred to as CInA (ZS) (or Ours (ZS)).

Intuition of What CInA (ZS) Learns.
CInA (ZS) is trained on multiple datasets and learns how to balance in an amortized fashion via the SVM loss. During testing, it can infer causal effects in a zero-shot manner, as it acquired the ability to directly infer the optimal balancing weights on a new dataset.
The transformation that encodes for V approximates the solution to the optimization problem in the primal SVM. Thus Algorithm 2 can be seen as learning to debias an observational dataset by learning to how optimize, which enjoys fast inference on a new dataset. It is worth noting that as our optimization problem is continuous and easier to solve than combinatorial optimization, we do not need to employ techniques such as reinforcement learning. We also do not require ground-truth labels to any individual optimization problems as the parameters are learned fully end-to-end.

Algorithm 2: CInA (multi-dataset version).
Input: Training datasets D^{(1)},...,D^{(M)}.
Hyper-parameter: penalty weight λ>0.
Parameters: θ (including φ), step size η.
while not converged do
    for m in [M] do
        Compute K,V using forward pass.
        Update θ ← θ - η ∇ L_θ(D^{(m)}).
    end for
end while

Algorithm 3: Direct Inference with CInA.
Input: Test dataset D^{(*)}, trained model, used penalty weight λ.
Output: Estimated sample average treatment effect \hat{τ}.
Compute h(X^{(*)}), V^{(*)} using forward pass.
Compute α* = λ · V^{(*)} / (h(X^{(*)}) W^{(*)}).
return \hat{τ} = (α* W^{(*)})^T Y^{(*)}.

Computational Complexity
We now discuss the computational complexity of our proposed method with respect to the number of units N in each dataset. Suppose the last attention layer uses keys and queries of dimension D. Inside each iteration of every epoch, since it needs to compute exp(k_i k_j / √D) for each pair of units i,j and h(X_i) for each i, the total complexity of this layer is O(N^2 D). Based on the outputs of the forward pass, the complexity to evaluate the loss function is O(N^2), as it evolves computing the penalty term. During inference, the complexity relies on the complexity of the forward pass, as computing α* and \hat{τ} are O(N).

Experiments
Our objectives are twofold: to validate our theoretical findings in a traditional single-dataset setting, and to evaluate the feasibility of CInA in a causal foundation modeling context, where the multi-dataset version of CInA will be used for zero-shot causal inference across settings with different levels of difficulty.

Simulation Study A: fixed causal graph
Base Setting. We follow the simulation study setting in Tarr et al. (2021), Lee et al. (2010), and Setoguchi et al. (2008) with some modifications. The main purpose of this experiment is to validate our theoretical findings by showing that CInA can perform competitively compared to baselines in the traditional single-dataset setting. We consider a synthetic dataset generated using a fixed causal graph. The covariates of each unit, X_i, are drawn from a 10-dimensional multivariate Gaussian distribution with 4 pairs of correlations introduced. Then the treatment is modeled as a single binary variable generated via a logistic model P(T_i=1|X_i) = sigmoid(η^T h(X_i)), where η is a randomly sampled coefficient parameter, and h is a moderately non-linear and non-additive function detailed in Setoguchi et al. (2008). Finally, the outcome variable is modeled as Y(T) = γ_0 + γ^T x + τ T + ε with ε ∼ N(0, 0.1) and τ = -0.4 (which defines the ATE). For this setting, we generate 100 different datasets sharing the same parameters, each containing 1024 units. We train all baselines, and the single-dataset version of CInA in Section 4.1, on each of these 100 datasets separately, and evaluate their overall performance. We refer to this setting as the single-mechanism setting. We also consider three harder variations to this base setting, detailed below.

Variation 1. In this variation, we aim to evaluate how the multi-dataset version of CInA performs in a zero-shot inference setting with moderate difficulty. We generate 100 different datasets (split into 60/20/20 for training/validation/testing). For each dataset, we first sample a new coefficient parameter η from a fixed random distribution p(η). We then generate 1024 units using the same form of outcome model specified in the base setting but with a different η for each dataset. Our multi-dataset model, CInA (ZS), is trained on 60 training datasets, with hyperparameters selected using 20 validation sets. The evaluation of its zero-shot performance is based on 20 testing datasets. All other baselines are still trained on a dataset-specific manner, i.e., they will be fit to the 20 testing sets separately. We refer to this setting as the multi-mechanism setting.

Variation 2. In the second variation, similar to variation 1, We generate 100 different datasets, each using a different coefficient parameter η from some prior distribution p(η). However, instead of sharing the same prior distribution for η, we force the training/validation datasets and testing datasets to have different supports for η, i.e., supp(p_training(η))= supp(p_validation(η)) ≠ supp(p_testing(η)). We refer to this setting as multi+OOD.

Variation 3. The third variation is the same as variation 2, except that the 100 datasets have different numbers of units, ranging from (512, 1024). This setting is referred to as Multi+OOD+diff_size.

Baselines (references) and Metrics. As previous methods are designed for a single dataset, we used them as reference for evaluating our zero-shot method. We consider the following baselines: the naive estimator, that performs covariate balancing with uniform weights in A; the IPW estimator, which performs classical inverse probability weighting with logistic models; the self-normalized IPW estimator that normalizes the IPW weights to be in A; the double machine learning (DML) estimator with a linear final stage model; and finally, the SVM approach which directly solves the dual SVM as quadratic programming on a per-dataset basis. Among those baselines, the parameter λ for SVM was selected using validation datasets, whenever available. When λ is selected properly, the SVM solution should give the exact solution and serve as the ground truth reference for the gradient-based methods, CInA and CInA-(ZS). To quantify the accuracy of causal inference, we use mean absolute error (MAE) between true ATE and predicted ATE as the main evaluation metric.
Results. Figure 3 shows the results for 4 different settings of simulation A. We observed that across all settings, the single dataset version of CInA consistently give on-par performance with DML, despite the unfair advantage of DML since it utilizes the outcome variables during training. CInA outperforms all other re-weighting based methods except for the ground truth reference, SVM. This further confirms the validity of our theoretical findings. Furthermore, in the multi-dataset settings (Multi-mechanism, Multi+OOD and Multi+OOD+diff_size), CInA (ZS) shows good zero-shot generalization capabilities under moderate causal mechanism shifts, and performs competitively against other baselines that are trained on the testing datasets themselves on a per-dataset basis.

Simulation Study B: Multiple Causal Graphs
In Simulation A, we validated our methods in both traditional single-dataset setting and moderate zero-shot settings under the assumption that all tasks/datasets share the same causal graph. Nevertheless, in an ideal context of causal foundational modeling, a good model should be able to perform zero-shot causal inference on datasets coming from both different graphs and different functional relationships. Therefore, in this section, we generate a large number of random synthetic datasets with randomly sampled causal graphs to further evaluate the capability of CInA.

Datasets.
Following Lachapelle et al. (2019), we generate 5000 datasets (referred to as the ER-5000 dataset) each using a different random Erdős-Rényi DAG. All datasets are pre-standardized and split into a 60/20/20 ratio for training/validation/testing. Similar to above, CInA (ZS) and CInA (ZS-S) (described below) are trained on training datasets, with hyperparameters selected based on validation sets. Reported statistics are based on testing datasets. All baselines are trained on each testing dataset individually.

Baselines (references) and Metrics. The baselines considered in this experiment are the same as Simulation A, with the exception that the DML baseline performs additional model selection from linear DML, kernel DML, and causal forest DML. We add another baseline designed for ER-5000, dubbed as mean prediction, which uses the mean ATE across all training datasets as the prediction for testing datasets. This helps us examine whether CInA is simply memorizing the ATEs from the training set. In addition to the evaluation metric used Simulation A, we evaluate the computational run-time of all methods on testing datasets.

Supervised Training of CInA. Unlike Simulation A, all datasets in ER-5000 have different average treatment effects. This allows us to utilize the ground truth ATEs of training datasets as additional supervised signals. We incorporate this via simultaneously minimizing ∑_{m in [M]} ‖ (V^{(m)} / h(X^{(m)}))^T Y^{(m)} - τ^{(m)} ‖^2. The new loss function hence becomes
∑_{m in [M]} L_θ (D^{(m)}) + μ ∑_{m in [M]} ‖ (V^{(m)} / h(X^{(m)}))^T Y^{(m)} - τ^{(m)} ‖^2,
where μ is the adjustable coefficient with default value 1. We refer to this supervised variation of our method as CInA (ZS-S) (or Ours (ZS-S)).

Results. Figure 4 summarizes the results on ER-5000 datasets. We observe that the unsupervised version of CInA (ZS) already reached the performance of DML, while being able to significantly accelerate the inference computational time by a magnitude of ∼10^2 (Figure 6). With additional supervised signals, CInA (ZS-S) is able to significantly outperforms all per-dataset baselines.

Empirical Studies on Real-world Datasets
Datasets and Baselines (references). We evaluate treatment effect estimation performances on real-world datasets including: Twins, IHDP, IHDP-resampled, ACIC, LaLonde CPS and LaLonde PSID. Among them, IHDP-resampled and ACIC naturally come with multiple datasets, hence can be used to evaluate the zero-shot causal inference for CInA (ZS). For other datasets, only the single dataset version of CInA is evaluated due to their single-causal mechanism nature. All baselines and cross-validation settings are the same as Simulation B.

Results. Figure 5 summarizes our results. We observe that the experimental findings in simulation studies also hold in real-world settings. In single-dataset experiments, CInA is able to outperform the majority of per-dataset baselines in most cases (except for DML in LaLonde PSID and IPW in Twins, etc). In multi-dataset experiments, namely, IHDP-resampled and ACIC, CInA (ZS) outperforms the majority of baselines including CInA. Furthermore, we noticed that unlike in simulations, SVM is not working well in IHDP-resampled and ACIC. This is potentially because the hyper-parameter selection is performed on validation datasets, which by construction, do not represent the causal graphs/functional relationships of the IHDP/ACIC test datasets well. However, our results show that CInA (ZS) and CInA (ZS-S) are able to robustly perform zero-shot causal inference on unseen datasets in this case. In summary, CInA and its variations generally perform well in real-world settings, however its performance may be limited by the availability of dataset resources.

Discussion
In this work, we take a pioneering first step towards building causally-aware foundation models for complex tasks, with a particular focus on the duality between causal inference and attention mechanisms in transformer-based architectures. In theory, we show that covariate balancing can be solved via training any neural network with self-attention as its last layer. Our proposed approach, Causal Inference with Attention (CInA), leverages multiple unlabeled datasets and is capable of performing zero-shot causal inference on unseen data. This stands in marked contrast to previous approaches, which need to re-optimize on new data. Empirical results show that CInA generalizes well to out-of-distribution datasets and various real-world datasets, reaching and even surpassing the performance of traditional per-dataset causal inference approaches. Therefore, we believe that our methods can serve as a promising and novel stepping stone towards causally-aware foundation models.

Going forward, we view it as an important future step to extend the scope of empirical efforts for obtaining a fully pretrained causal foundation model. First, much work remains to be done to build large (public) datasets incorporating large-scale real-world/semi-synthetic data. Second, it would be crucial to improve the efficiency of our method, potentially incorporating techniques from efficient transformers.
